articles.title: AI error nearly led US to seize Chinese ship: ‘Almost started a war’
articles.body:
A faulty intelligence report produced with the help of artificial intelligence and circulated throughout the U.S. military during the war in Iran nearly led the United States to launch a military operation against a Chinese vessel — and could have sparked a confrontation between the two powers, CNN reported Friday, citing people familiar with the incident.
According to the report, the episode took place last spring, when an intelligence assessment reaching U.S. military officials concluded that a Chinese vessel in the Middle East was carrying components linked to a nuclear weapons development program. The information immediately raised serious concerns, prompting the military to begin preparing to intercept the ship.
Four sources who spoke with CNN said preparations had reached an advanced stage: Armed U.S. personnel were preparing to board the vessel and military aircraft were already in the air.
Only shortly before the planned operation did officials decide to scrutinize the intelligence report more closely. They then discovered it had been prepared with the help of artificial intelligence and that a chatbot used by the analyst had incorrectly identified the material the ship was carrying.
CNN said it was unable to determine what the vessel’s cargo actually contained.
One source described the report as “entirely false,” adding: “It almost started a war.”
According to CNN, U.S. action against a Chinese vessel could have triggered a serious escalation and potentially an armed confrontation between Washington and Beijing. The network said the episode illustrates a more immediate danger than the extreme scenarios senior technology executives have warned about in recent weeks: not AI “going out of control,” but humans making potentially momentous decisions based on false information it generates.
The report was prepared by an analyst at Special Operations Command. According to CNN, the analyst entered intelligence about the ship’s cargo manifest into a chatbot, using information originating from U.S. Special Operations Command Pacific, which is headquartered in Hawaii.
It was unclear whether the analyst used a commercial chatbot or a system developed for the U.S. government. The system combined information from open sources with classified signals intelligence stored in government databases and reached the incorrect conclusion about the cargo.
The analyst then used artificial intelligence again, this time to turn the findings into the standard format of an official intelligence report — the kind of document military decision-makers are accustomed to treating as a reliable source — and circulated it.
A former senior U.S. official familiar with the artificial intelligence systems used by defense and intelligence agencies said internal government tools are not necessarily fundamentally different from commercial AI products.
U.S. Special Operations Command Pacific and the Pentagon did not respond to CNN’s requests for comment.
The episode comes as the U.S. military and intelligence community accelerate the adoption of artificial intelligence across nearly every aspect of their work, from analyzing vast quantities of intelligence and selecting targets to budgeting, logistics and supply chain management.
The goal is to allow the military to make decisions more quickly, in part because of concerns that the United States could fall behind China and other rivals in the use of the technology.
In January, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth unveiled the Pentagon’s “AI Acceleration Strategy,” aimed at removing barriers and rapidly expanding the use of the technology so it would be available to roughly 3 million military personnel and civilian employees across all classification levels.
The plan included projects to integrate AI into battlefield management, intelligence and decision-making.
At the program’s launch, Hegseth said the United States would “unleash experimentation, eliminate bureaucratic barriers, focus our investments” to ensure U.S. leadership in military artificial intelligence.
But U.S. officials said implementation of AI systems is taking place in a decentralized way, with different parts of the military and intelligence community using different tools under inconsistent instructions and safety standards.
They said there is currently no single set of rules defining how AI-generated information must be verified before it is used in operational decision-making.
Concern is particularly acute when it comes to target selection.
A person familiar with military policy told CNN that the use of AI in targeting is “definitely something that is ramping up,” but said clear guidelines still do not exist to ensure that keeping a human in the decision-making process will actually prevent civilian casualties or friendly fire.
The AI “hallucination” — the term used when an AI system produces information that sounds credible but is false — that led to the Chinese ship episode was not an isolated case, according to one source.
Several veteran intelligence officials said the technology is increasing pressure on analysts to produce and distribute intelligence quickly, raising the risk of mistakes. They said younger analysts who have grown accustomed to using such tools may also be more inclined to trust them without sufficient scrutiny.
“AI allows you to get to a bad idea faster,” one source said.
Another sensitive China incident: F-35 parts reached Hong Kong
Alongside the faulty intelligence report, U.S. authorities have opened an investigation into another sensitive security incident involving China: A shipment of parts from an F-35 stealth fighter, which was being sent from Australia to the United States for repairs, was unexpectedly diverted to Hong Kong, Politico reported Friday.
According to three people familiar with the matter, the components were being shipped on behalf of aircraft manufacturer Lockheed Martin through an intermediary, but during their journey across the Pacific the shipment arrived in Hong Kong instead of the United States.
It remains unclear why the shipment’s route was changed or who currently has possession of the parts, according to the report.
The Pentagon confirmed there was an issue involving a shipment of unserviceable F-35 components.
The F-35 program office said it was working with U.S. authorities and industry partners “to recover the components, investigate the incident and implement safeguards to prevent a recurrence.”
The incident has prompted an investigation on Capitol Hill and a series of briefings for congressional committees dealing with national security.
According to the sources, State Department and Pentagon officials began briefing congressional staff on the matter in June, with additional briefings expected in the coming weeks.
The main concern centers on the type of components included in the shipment.
Two of the sources said the parts included an F-35 cockpit canopy containing technology related to the aircraft’s stealth capabilities that is available only to the United States and its allies.
The canopy is a transparent acrylic shell covering the cockpit and is coated with a thin, transparent layer of radar-absorbing material designed to reduce the aircraft’s radar signature and make it more difficult for enemy systems to detect.
U.S. officials are concerned that if such a component fell into the hands of an adversary, it could be closely examined and parts of the technology could potentially be reverse-engineered.
The fact that the shipment reached Hong Kong has heightened concerns that China could gain access to the components.
Beijing has long been accused of trying to obtain information about sensitive U.S. weapons programs, including the F-35.
“It’s no secret that China has been aggressively trying to get F-35 data through electronic espionage, among other means,” J.J. Gertler, a former House Armed Services Committee staffer and military aviation analyst at the Congressional Research Service, told Politico.
Gertler said that even if Beijing already possesses specifications or other information about the parts, having access to an actual component could allow it to verify and improve the information it already has.
Lockheed Martin said it could not comment on the status of shipments for security reasons but stressed that it complies with all U.S. regulations governing the transfer of aircraft components.
The company added that its personnel handle every shipment “with the utmost diligence and safeguards” to protect the security of the F-35 program and participating allies.
The F-35 program is one of the largest and most expensive weapons programs in U.S. history. Along with supply chain problems and spare-parts shortages, it has for years struggled with high maintenance costs and difficulties meeting readiness targets for the aircraft fleet.
The episode also highlights a longstanding problem in the F-35 program’s vast and complex supply chain, which relies on maintenance and repair facilities in multiple countries as well as commercial shipping companies.
Countries participating in the program use a shared global pool of spare parts, which remain Pentagon property until they are installed on aircraft but are, in practice, managed largely by contractors.
A 2023 report by the U.S. Government Accountability Office found that more than 1 million F-35 spare parts, worth tens of millions of dollars, had been classified as lost over roughly five years.
The watchdog criticized the Pentagon’s limited ability to track the parts, in part because much of the relevant information is held by contractors that manage the supply system.

Elsewhere, Saudi Arabia on Friday and early Saturday warned of a “hostile aerial threat” and issued a string of emergency alerts across the kingdom, as fighting with Yemen's Houthi rebels escalates.
48 killed in Yemen fighting between Houthis, gvnt forces

Israel kills son of renowned Gaza health ministry director

Iran's judiciary announced on Saturday the execution of a man accused of providing information about Iranian missile sites to Israeli intelligence.

articles.title: Lying to its people, denying its crimes
articles.body:
Lying to its people, denying its crimes
Seven months of concealment: the price Americans aren't told, the crimes Iranians won't forget
TEHRAN — Seven months after the United States and Israel launched their war against Iran, a growing body of reporting, congressional scrutiny, military documents and international investigations is exposing a widening gap between Washington’s public narrative of the conflict and the scale of its human, military and financial consequences.
The war began on February 28 with Washington and Tel Aviv presenting the destruction of Iran’s nuclear and missile capabilities as central objectives. President Donald Trump repeatedly said Iran could not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon and, immediately after the opening strikes, described the operation as necessary to prevent that outcome.
Yet the premise of an imminent nuclear threat has remained contested. The Arms Control Association noted that, at the time of the February attack, neither Trump nor Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu publicly presented evidence of an ongoing Iranian nuclear-weapons effort, while International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi said in early March that the agency did not see a structured program to manufacture nuclear weapons.
Trump nevertheless repeatedly suggested that the conflict would be short. In early March, he said that Iran would have had a nuclear weapon had the United States not acted within two weeks, while subsequent reporting documented a series of shifting predictions about when the war would end. By September, the conflict had entered its seventh month.
Against that backdrop, the question increasingly confronting Washington is not simply what the war has achieved, but how much of its human and material cost has been fully disclosed.
Civilian casualties and the Minab investigation
The most consequential challenge to the official narrative concerns the February 28 strike on the Shajareh Tayyebeh school in Minab, southern Iran.
A recent investigation by the United Nations Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran found “reasonable grounds” to believe that the United States committed a war crime in the Minab strike and in a separate attack on a sports complex and residential area in Lamerd. The mission said the two attacks killed at least 178 civilians.
The Minab attack became one of the war’s most devastating incidents, killing many civilians, including more than 100 children. UN findings said the school was a clearly identifiable civilian facility and that US forces had failed to take the necessary measures to establish that it was a legitimate military target.
The significance of the findings goes beyond the death toll. They challenge the explanation that the Minab strike was simply an unavoidable consequence of the fog of war.
A separate investigation reported by Bloomberg has shed further light on the military decision-making that preceded the attack. According to the investigation, Pentagon investigators identified flawed intelligence, outdated imagery and excessive reliance on artificial-intelligence systems as factors that contributed to the strike that killed 123 children.
The emerging picture is therefore one in which the tragedy cannot readily be reduced to a single technical error. Questions have instead been raised about the entire targeting process — from the intelligence entering the system to the human decisions made after it was processed.
For Tehran, Minab has become a symbol of the civilian toll of the war. Internationally, the UN findings have transformed the incident from an Iranian allegation into the subject of a formal international investigation and legal assessment.
Washington, however, has rejected the UN mission's conclusions. The White House and State Department have disputed the findings and questioned the mission's impartiality.
That disagreement does not resolve the underlying issue: whether the full US investigation into Minab should be made public.
Kuhestak: another strike, another demand for answers
The question of transparency has gained renewed urgency following the September 1 strike on a home in Kuhestak, Hormozgan Province, where a wedding gathering was taking place.
Six Democratic senators — Brian Schatz, Patty Murray, Jeanne Shaheen, Jack Reed, Mark Warner and Chris Coons — have called for a “fully and impartially” conducted investigation into the attack.
The lawmakers said reports indicated that four civilians, including women and a child, were killed and more than 60 people wounded, and that weapons experts and visual analysis suggested the strike was caused by a US bomb. They demanded that the Pentagon release its findings to Congress and the American public.
The senators also said Congress had yet to receive the full findings of the Pentagon's investigation into the February 28 Minab strike.
Their intervention is significant because it places the issue of civilian casualties inside the US political system itself. The demand is not coming only from foreign governments or international organizations; members of the Senate are asking the Pentagon to disclose what it knows about the conduct and consequences of American military operations.
The Kuhestak case therefore adds a second, more recent test of Washington's commitment to transparency.
A casualty count under scrutiny
The questions surrounding transparency extend beyond Iranian civilian deaths.
On September 18, The Washington Post reported that more American service members had died during the Iran war than the Pentagon had publicly acknowledged.
Five US officials familiar with the Defense Department's internal casualty accounting told the newspaper that at least 22 US military personnel had died — four more than the number appearing in the Pentagon's public casualty database. A sixth official put the figure at 23, although that person said not all of the additional deaths were directly attributable to combat and involved US personnel deployed in the Middle East during the hostilities.
The same official said three US contractors in the region had also died since combat operations began.
The Pentagon declined to address the discrepancy in the figures, according to the newspaper.
The issue is not merely statistical. The Pentagon's public casualty database serves as the official record of military deaths and provides the public with information about the human cost of US military operations.
The Washington Post reported that, as of September 18, the public database listed 18 US military fatalities since the beginning of the conflict, while more than 820 service members had been wounded.
Discrepancy has therefore raised a basic question: if the Pentagon's internal accounting contains additional deaths, why are they not reflected in the public record?
What the photographs of US bases reveal
Another part of the story has emerged from photographs taken inside American military installations across the Middle East.
CBS News recently obtained photographs from active-duty US service members showing extensive damage at American positions in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and elsewhere following Iranian missile and drone attacks.
The images included damaged buildings and vehicles at Camp Buehring and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait and severe damage to an E-3 Sentry aircraft at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia. CBS said the photographs were provided by serving military personnel who spoke anonymously because of military restrictions on the media.
The Pentagon's inspector general has separately reported equipment losses worth up to $3.7 billion, including losses involving nearly 60 aircraft, while recording Iranian attacks on US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
The photographs matter because they provide a visual record of damage that is difficult to capture in official statements consisting largely of aggregate figures.
They also complicate the image of an American military campaign conducted with overwhelming protection from retaliation.
One US service member quoted by CBS described the situation in stark terms, saying the damage being inflicted on American bases had not been adequately communicated to the public.
Other reporting has independently documented damage to American aircraft. CBS reported that an A-10 at a US base in Jordan lost a wing in an Iranian strike, while several F-15s sustained damage.
The bill comes to $43.6 billion — and counting
The most tangible measure of the war's cost is financial.
According to an updated estimate from US Central Command provided to Congress, the conflict had cost the United States approximately $43.6 billion by September 3. About $28.1 billion of the total was attributed to expended munitions. The estimate does not include damage to US bases across the region.
The figure represents a substantial increase from the Congressional Budget Office's estimate of approximately $38 billion through August 1.
The CBO has projected that the war could continue adding roughly $3 billion a month, depending on the intensity of military operations.
The most striking element of the new estimate is the cost of weapons. US munitions expenditure rose from approximately $21.7 billion in the earlier CBO calculation to about $28.1 billion in the Central Command estimate.
The financial burden comes alongside pressure on American weapons stocks. The CBO has warned that the conflict has consumed substantial quantities of precision weapons and missile interceptors, potentially creating replenishment challenges for years.
For a war whose stated objective was to remove a strategic threat, the depletion of American military stocks has itself become a strategic concern.
A war is increasingly difficult to measure through official statements
The emerging evidence does not establish that every undisclosed casualty, military loss or omission was deliberately concealed. Some discrepancies may reflect classification rules, changing casualty categories, operational security or the normal lag involved in military investigations.
But the accumulation of discrepancies has become difficult to ignore.
Civilian deaths in Iran have generated UN investigations and congressional demands for disclosure. American military fatalities appear to exceed the numbers contained in the Pentagon's public database. Photographs from US service members reveal damage at bases that was not initially visible in official accounts. Pentagon documents show billions of dollars in equipment and munitions losses, while the overall cost of the war has risen to $43.6 billion.
At the same time, the Trump administration continues to seek additional resources for the military. The administration has proposed a $1.5 trillion defense budget, while also seeking additional funding connected to the Iran war and other defense priorities.
The result is an increasingly difficult contradiction for Washington: the longer the war continues, the harder it becomes to contain its consequences within a simple narrative of a rapid and decisive military operation.
 
 Seven months into the conflict, the central question is no longer only what the United States says happened in Iran.
It is what the accumulating evidence — from UN investigators, American lawmakers, Pentagon documents, US military personnel and American media investigations — says happened after the first bombs fell.
And on that question, the record is becoming considerably larger than the official daily casualty figures, battlefield statements and headline claims of success.

articles.body:

According to government officials, multiple European nations anticipate significant postponements in receiving contracted air defense assets and precision-strike missile systems.

Officials added that several Eastern European countries reliant on American defense hardware began experiencing delivery delays shortly after the US initiated military combat operations against Iran in February 2026.

AfD Leaders Plan Talks With Putin Envoy on Russian Gas
European procurement delays
The Pentagon’s prioritization of domestic stockpile reconstitution has complicated Ukrainian and European efforts to reinforce Ukrainian airspace protection ahead of anticipated winter Russian bombardments.
Despite broader supply constraints, the US continues to facilitate deliveries of arms procured for Ukraine by European allies through EU and NATO financing frameworks.
European leaders plan to approach US President Donald Trump during next week’s United Nations General Assembly in New York to lobby for additional Patriot interceptor allocations for Ukraine.
In addition, EU officials are seeking to negotiate production licensing agreements that would permit European manufacturers to produce Patriot missiles domestically to supply Kyiv’s defense requirements.
US operations in the Middle East consumed more than 1,500 Patriot interceptors, leaving total US inventory at fewer than 1,700 units. The inventory drawdown has constrained the availability of long-range precision assets, including Army Tactical Missile Systems (ATACMS) and Precision Strike Missiles (PrSM).
Production bottlenecks
In response to the supply strain, the US Department of Defense has directed US defense contractors to accelerate serial production lines. Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell confirmed that the department is working to compress procurement schedules to meet expanding operational requirements.
US Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg reportedly issued a formal directive to prime defense contractors demanding actionable acceleration plans within 21 days, stating that multi-year development timelines are unacceptable given prevailing geopolitical conditions.
The strategic redirection of munitions has also affected the US force posture in the Indo-Pacific. To sustain Middle East operations, the Pentagon redeployed hundreds of interceptors, advanced naval destroyers, a carrier strike group, and Tomahawk inventories from the US Indo-Pacific Command, drawing down regional assets previously stationed in South Korea and Japan.

articles.title: North Korea’s HIMARS-style launcher moves into production
articles.body:
- North Korean state media said Kim Jong Un toured munitions factories from Sept. 16 to 18, inspecting production tied to a rocket launcher resembling the U.S. HIMARS system.
- The visit follows a May 2026 test of the launcher alongside an upgraded 240mm rocket and an AI-guided cruise missile Kim ordered deployed near the South Korean border.
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un toured major munitions factories over three days, from Sept. 16 to 18, inspecting weapons production that reportedly included a mobile rocket launcher Western analysts have compared to the U.S. Army’s HIMARS system, state media reported Sept. 19.
The ruling Workers’ Party newspaper Rodong Sinmun said Kim, the party’s general secretary, visited “important munitions industry enterprises” to check on production conditions. Kim told factory officials the military must “constantly load the most powerful and overwhelming strategic force” into the armed forces, according to the report, and pressed the plants to expand output.
The visit follows a pattern Kim has repeated for years, touring weapons factories every few months and calling for faster, larger-scale production. He made similar visits in August 2023, January 2024 and December 2025, each time emphasizing what state media described as the “paramount importance” of missile and artillery output to the country’s war readiness.
The launcher system tied to this week’s visit first appeared publicly at a 2023 military parade and was tested for the first time on May 26, 2026, alongside two other weapons: an upgraded 240mm guided rocket and a tactical cruise missile North Korea says uses artificial intelligence for terminal guidance.
Photos released by North Korean state media at the time showed a wheeled vehicle carrying a small number of launch tubes, a configuration that resembles the U.S. Army’s M142 HIMARS, a truck-mounted system that fires precision-guided rockets from a single launcher and has seen extensive combat use in Ukraine. South Korea’s military detected the May test independently, tracking projectiles that flew roughly 80 km (50 miles) toward the Yellow Sea, though Seoul did not confirm North Korea’s specific claims about the systems involved.
Kim ordered the accelerated deployment of the AI-guided cruise missile to front-line artillery units near the South Korean border after that May test, calling the results “a clear signal” of North Korea’s military progress. This week’s factory tour suggests the program has moved from testing toward production, though North Korea did not disclose how many units of any system have been built or where the factories are located, following its usual practice of withholding exact locations from state media coverage.
The factory visit came the same week North Korea rejected a resolution the International Atomic Energy Agency adopted criticizing its nuclear weapons program. North Korean officials said the country’s status as a nuclear power is permanently written into domestic law and does not require international recognition, a position Pyongyang has maintained consistently in response to IAEA and U.N. criticism.

articles.title: North Korea has fired around 150 ballistic missiles at Ukraine, learning from each one. Same missiles threaten Japan, and Kyiv just shows its speaker what is inside them
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Intelligence, also known as HUR, has given Japan's parliament speaker a rare, close look at a North Korean weapon: the components of a ballistic missile Russia fired at Ukraine. Ukrainian officers have shown the parts to Eisuke Mori, speaker of Japan's House of Representatives, during his delegation's visit to Kyiv, HUR says on social media.
Ukraine has become the place where North Korea's missiles are tested in combat and taken apart. Pyongyang has supplied Russia with roughly 150 KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles since late 2023, along with thousands of troops, and Russia has fired scores of them at Ukrainian cities.
Each strike gives Pyongyang combat data that has sharpened its weapons. Showing Japan the components turns that access into a prospect of future deterrence: the same missiles threaten the Asia-Pacific.
Ukraine hands Japan the evidence
Examining missile parts allows analysts to read the missile's technical characteristics, design, and the state of North Korea's arms industry, HUR says. Ukraine has found that the North Korean missiles falling on its cities are built partly from foreign parts, with components traced to companies in Britain, Japan, Switzerland, China, and the US, Radio Free Asia reports, evidence of how Pyongyang skirts sanctions to build them.
The threat reaches the Pacific
HUR frames the demonstration as a shared-security case. North Korean weapons endanger not only Ukraine but Japan and the wider Asia-Pacific, it says, while the Moscow-Pyongyang partnership lets Russia keep waging its war and lets Pyongyang build up its arsenal and refine its weapons.
"Countering this cooperation requires coordinated action by international partners. Sharing intelligence helps better assess common threats and find ways to overcome them," HUR states.
Pyongyang learns from the strikes
North Korea has sent Russia millions of artillery shells, rocket systems, and thousands of troops, and is paid in cash and technology, with one analyst estimating Pyongyang may have earned about $20 billion from the war. In return, the missiles' accuracy has improved as Pyongyang studies how they perform under fire, turning the war into a live proving ground for weapons built to threaten its neighbors.

articles.title: US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortages –  Bloomberg
articles.body:
US warns allies of missile delivery delays due to shortages – Bloomberg
The US has warned allies to expect delays of up to five years in the delivery of key types of weaponry, as the country works to replenish its own stockpiles, which have been depleted.
Source: Bloomberg, as reported by European Pravda
Details: According to officials, a number of European countries expect deliveries of key missile systems and air defence assets to be delayed as a result of the US armed forces depleting their own arsenal during the war with Iran.
It is reported that Germany has asked the US to speed up the delivery of long-range Tomahawk cruise missiles and Typhon ground-based launchers, but the depleted US stockpiles of this powerful weaponry mean its manufacturer, Raytheon, is unlikely to be able to fulfil the order within the next five years.
Two further officials said some Eastern European countries, which also rely on American weapons systems, had already encountered delays shortly after the US and Israel launched a war against Iran on 28 February.
The Pentagon's decision to prioritise its own stockpiles is also complicating Ukraine's efforts to get the US to send it more Patriot interceptors ahead of what is expected to be a harsh winter.
The question of the air defence system Ukraine urgently needs will be a key topic at United Nations meetings taking place in New York next week.
It is estimated that the US used more than half of its most advanced Patriot missiles, a third of its Tomahawk missiles, and nearly half of its precision-strike missiles and THAAD interceptors in Iran. The Congressional Budget Office said that, since June 2025, the US has likely used as much as two-thirds of its missile defence interceptor stockpiles.
The shortage of stockpiles is affecting not only the US and Europe. In April, the US told Japan that Tomahawk missile deliveries will be delayed by up to two years. Saudi Arabia has also called on allies, including the US, to provide military support to repel Houthi attacks in Yemen. Washington has not said whether it will provide additional assistance.
However, according to sources, the US is continuing to supply weapons purchased by European allies for Ukraine as part of NATO and European Union initiatives.
Background:
- CNN reported earlier that the United States has used around 80% of its available stockpiles for a key air defence system, with military officials warning that its warehouse levels are "dangerously low".
- Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth denied media reports that the US armed forces are running low on stockpiles of key missiles.

articles.title: The US air force admitted to deploying weapons in space. Don’t expect the White House to explain why
articles.body:
In Hollywood at least, space weapons are a relatively simple concept. The good guys, from Captain Kirk and his crew in Star Trek, to Luke Skywalker’s rebel alliance in Star Wars, battle intergalactic villains with an array of colorful lasers and particle-beam cannons, then the bad guys get dispatched in a spectacular, explosive finale.
The messaging coming out of the White House on the subject, by contrast, could not be more vague.
This week’s attention-grabbing revelation by air force secretary Troy Meink – that the US has deployed some kind of weapons in space – carried nothing in the way of context or detail, and left experts scratching their heads at exactly what Donald Trump has in his cosmic arsenal. And, equally importantly, what he intends to do with it.
“You can count the words, and the disclosure, on one hand, so there’s not much there to work with, and we really don’t know what kind of weapons he was talking about,” Clayton Swope, deputy director of the aerospace security project and a senior fellow in the defense and security department at the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), said of Meink’s announcement.
“The US is looking for another tool to deter what it sees as concerning Russian and Chinese behaviors in space, so my guess is that revealing it has on-orbit weapons would be your way to do that.
“[But] that level of detail needed to make this disclosure effective as a deterrent isn’t there. It could just be a building block, and the US is going to lay out more later with that. To me that would make logical sense, if that was the plan.”
What the plan actually is has never been made clear, and Meink, in his announcement, stressed it was unlikely ever to be.
“Me talking about the details of what we’re doing would actually not benefit deterrence, so we’re not going to talk about the specifics of what we’re doing, whether we’ve tested it, not tested it, or anything else,” he said.
But as Russia and China, both US adversaries, have advanced their own aggressive outer space ambitions and agendas, Trump has responded by placing an ever-increasing focus on militarizing the heavens.
During his first term of office, he created Space Force, the first new, separate branch of the US military in more than seven decades. Last month, he signed an executive order designating the first US Space Academy, a proposed joint civilian-military institution modeled on the army and navy training academies at West Point and Annapolis, to be sited at an as-yet unnamed location.
This week, Military Times reported plans to recruit and train 10,000 new guardians, as Space Force service members are known, to join uniformed ranks within the next five years.
Gen Dan Caine, who as chair of the joint chiefs of staff is the country’s most senior military leader, told the Air, Space and Cyber Conference in Maryland this week, that the armed forces including Space Force must be “prepared to fight, endure and win … from the seabed to cislunar space”.
Added to a number of other maneuvers and bold pronouncements Trump has made concerning space in recent weeks and months, it is hard not to see the space weapons reveal by Meink – who holds a civilian position reporting to the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth – as a further blending of the traditionally separate military and non-military roles of US space policy.
In August, the White House unveiled a national space transportation policy that gives Hegseth, as head of the defense department, new responsibility and authority to determine with the chief of Nasa, Jared Isaacman, who manages all US space launches, and sets an ambitious, expansive federal target of more than 1,000 launch and reentry operations by 2030.
The president, meanwhile, has made no secret of his desire for US astronauts to beat China and land on the moon before he leaves office in January 2029; and in March laid out plans, arguably rooted more in optimism than expectation, to invest $20bn (£15bn) on a moonbase to secure for the US the first permanent foothold on the lunar surface.
Some analysts see an almost sea change in the way the Trump administration has approached space in pursuit of its geopolitical goals, compared to previous presidents who upheld decades of separation between the government’s civilian and military needs.
“The way that the US has structured it since Nasa was established in the late 1950s was we have a civil space organization focused on civil exploration, on science, and then we have the Pentagon,” Swope said.
He continued: “There seems to be a tendency to pull them together more than we’ve seen in the past [and] the creation of the Space Academy is just another data point that suggests that at least within the eyes of this administration, the missions are very not just complementary, but very, very similar.
“The civilian space agency and Pentagon, [it’s] not just that they complement each other, but that they’re essentially doing the same mission.”
Certainly, Trump has become more visible in space circles since inviting Isaacman, at the second time of asking, to lead Nasa. Seen as an ally of Elon Musk, the billionaire SpaceX chief and former political acolyte of the president, Isaacman has proven a staunch Trump loyalist in social media posts and in public appearances.
It was the “experience of a lifetime”, Isaacman gushed on X, to accompany Trump on Air Force One to the Johnson Space Center in Houston last month, where the academy announcement was staged before rows of Nasa’s civilian astronaut corps bedecked in their blue flight suits.
In a separate, lengthier post, Isaacman defended the need for a space academy with military theming, arguing that US ambitions necessitated “a bright new generation educated and prepared for this environment”.
He wrote: “If you understand the increasingly important and contested environment above us, then [the academy] is as timely and necessary today as the Space Force has already proven to be.”
The argument that the academy blurs the line between peaceful applications in space and the military, he said, “may be the weakest argument I have seen”, before chronicling a succession of previous Nasa missions and operations that were classified and defense department-based, and noting the agency’s early rockets were modified and evolved from military ballistic missiles.
“Nasa’s mission is as peaceful as it is patriotic,” he said. “We explore for the benefit of all humankind, but we go there under our flag. That mission would be impossible without the Guardians standing watch over the domain as we venture outward.”
Lori Garver, a former deputy administrator of Nasa during the Biden administration, said that while she saw the academy as potentially helpful to the US space program and its future workforce, she was concerned it conflated the agency’s mission for peaceful, civil space exploration with Space Force’s military goals.
“Nasa’s charter and legal foundation calls for a civilian agency separate from the military,” she told the science publication Ars Technica. “Structuring a feeder college along the lines of a military academy strikes me as ill-conceived.”
Others say it is difficult, or impossible, for the US to remain committed to the 1967 Outer Space treaty that mandated, among other regulations, that all nations use space for peaceful, non-militarized ends when some countries are blatantly defying it.
US intelligence agencies said in 2024 they were monitoring the development of a new Russian space weapon with the capability of shooting down satellites in Earth’s orbit. Lt Gen Gregory Gagnon, head of the Space Force combat forces command, told reporters at the Maryland conference that China was “actively pursuing activities in the system, in parts of space”, which the country has denied.
A Space Force “threat fact sheet” details how Russia and China are both “testing and fielding sophisticated counterspace capabilities with the intent to disrupt and degrade US space-enabled capabilities”.
So, to Swope, the CSIS analyst who worked for the Central Intelligence Agency’s directorate of science and technology for more than a decade, the US’s declaration that it had deployed space weapons of its own was more significant than the absence of detail.
“It’s this idea of space superiority, ‘I want to use space, I don’t want my adversary to’,” he said. “That’s just where we are today.
“Is more of that happening in space? I don’t think this announcement is determining that, or even accelerating that. It may be more just a recognition that the US has woken up to it, and we may just not know it because it’s not public.”
Another question, he said, is what kind of weapons the US may have. “It has talked previously about systems that operate in the electromagnetic spectrum, for jamming or interference with radio signals, that’s what we know publicly about what is in the US counter-space arsenal,” he said.
“War is really bad whether it is confined to Earth or orbit, and maybe we need to have a better thought not just on how we could limit specific types of weapons, but that we want to avoid generally.
“You can’t just walk into a quote-unquote space war and expect that not to be ugly.”

articles.title: Most NATO Allies Cannot Repel Russian Missile Attack, Latvia Says
articles.body:
Most NATO member states would be unable to intercept a Russian missile assault if the conflict broadens, and Europe is failing to keep pace with the rapid evolution of drone warfare in Ukraine, Latvian President Edgars Rinkēvičs warned.
According to The Guardian, Rinkēvičs stated that technological adaptations in unmanned systems and aerial combat are progressing at “lightning speed” on Ukrainian battlefields, cautioning that Western defense procurement and preparation timelines risk becoming obsolete by mid-2027.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“What we see is that air defense, drone defense, anti-ballistic defence has serious problems,” Rinkēvičs said. “And let’s be frank. Ukraine has it. The whole of Europe and NATO has it.”
The Latvian head of state emphasized that the alliance’s defensive gaps leave member nations exposed in the event of direct Russian escalation. “Because if Russia decides to use a couple of missiles in that territory, I think that would be a serious challenge today for many countries to cope with that,” he added.
Interceptor shortages
Rinkēvičs’s warning arrives as European allies and Ukraine confront severe bottlenecks in acquiring Patriot batteries and high-end surface-to-air interceptors.
According to analyses of Congressional Budget Office assessments, the US has expended nearly two-thirds of its critical interceptor inventories during military operations in the war against Iran, with defense planners estimating that replenishing American strategic reserves could require at least five years.
Luxembourg Airport Halts Flights Over Unauthorized Drones
While Washington has reviewed proposals to outsource Patriot missile production or license manufacturing to European and Ukrainian defense contractors, formal multilateral co-production frameworks have yet to be finalized.
“It’s up to the United States government, it’s up to the company,” Rinkēvičs noted, acknowledging the administrative and intellectual property hurdles involved in defense licensing. “We have some capacities in Europe, but let’s face it: Patriots are still one of the best, if not the best, to tackle this.”
Eastern flank warnings
The Latvian president’s assessment aligns with mounting concern across NATO’s eastern flank regarding deliberate Russian provocations and testing of allied collective defense commitments.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned the Polish parliament that intelligence dispatches indicate Russian operational blueprints include hybrid drone and missile strikes against nations supporting Kyiv, including Poland.
Tusk cautioned that Moscow could orchestrate strikes entering allied airspace while claiming they were accidental deviations, aiming to erode alliance cohesion and portray NATO’s Article 5 mutual defense guarantee as “more theoretical than practical.”
The warning followed consecutive incidents along Poland’s eastern frontier, including a Russian drone crashing within kilometers of Polish territory during an assault on western Ukraine.
Concurrently, US President Donald Trump stated to reporters on Friday, Sept. 18, that Russia has attacked Ukraine’s allies for “about five years,” treating Russian hybrid warfare, physical sabotage, and cross-border airspace breaches as an established reality facing European partners.

articles.title: US military estimates Iran war cost at $43.6 billion
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US military estimates Iran war cost at $43.6 billion
The US military's price tag for the Iran war has grown to $43.6 billion as of 3 September, according to a new estimate provided this week to lawmakers.
The figure from US Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched by the United States and Israel on 28 February.
A Congressional Budget Office report released Tuesday said the war had cost $38 billion through 1 August and will continue to rack up expenses of around $3 billion a month depending on the conflict's intensity.
The new breakdown, seen by The Associated Press and reported earlier by Punchbowl News, also showed the continued use of expensive munitions by American forces.
Weapons costs jumped by more than $6 billion in just over a month, from $21.7 billion listed in the CBO report to $28.1 billion in US Central Command’s estimate.
The financial cost is just one measure of the impact of the Iran war, which also is affecting oil prices and the stock market and has led to deaths and injuries of American troops.
The political costs will be calculated in November's midterm congressional elections, with Republicans facing increasing headwinds from the war's unpopularity.
The US military's one-page breakdown to Congress includes costs for operating warships, planes and bases as well as for equipment losses and medical support for troops.
Casualties tallied by the Pentagon have included 18 dead and more than 830 wounded, according to the Defense Casualty Analysis System.
The report does not include damage to US bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released Monday said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.
In the new report to Congress, the figure for munitions was by far the largest, constituting well over half of all costs. The advanced weapons that have been in the most demand are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army's Patriot and THAAD systems.
The diminished stockpiles also have caused alarm in Europe, where U.S. and NATO officials have told the AP that there is a “beyond critical” shortage of missile interceptors.
Saudi Arabia also is running low on interceptors and has turned to regional and Western allies for assistance as its standoff with Houthi rebels in Yemen drags on.
(The Associated Press)

articles.title: Putin approves takeover of French and Swiss giants’ Russian assets. Why now?
articles.body:
Putin approves takeover of French and Swiss giants’ Russian assets. Why now?
President Vladimir Putin has ordered the Russian subsidiaries of Nestle, Auchan and Leroy Merlin placed under temporary management owing to Western support for Ukrainian strikes on Russian civilian and economic infrastructure.
Moscow introduced the temporary management mechanism in 2023 in response to Western companies leaving Russia and the seizure of Russian state and private assets abroad. Officials said it was intended to keep strategically important businesses operating and shield the economy from decisions by “unfriendly” countries.
On Thursday, Putin amended the 2023 decree to add the Russian assets of Nestle, Auchan and Leroy Merlin to the list. All three were transferred to L.E.V. Management, a business and management consultancy.
Why now?
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the companies’ home countries and their support for Kiev were major factors behind the decision.
“We are talking about European companies, companies from unfriendly countries,” he told journalists on Friday. “These are unfriendly countries that are actively involved in military actions against our country,” Peskov said, adding that some also support Ukrainian strikes “against our civilian economic infrastructure.”
Why these companies?
Auchan and Leroy Merlin are controlled by France’s Mulliez family through ELO Group and ADEO respectively. Nestle’s Russian business was controlled by subsidiaries of the Swiss food giant.
France has been one of Kiev’s major military backers throughout the conflict. President Emmanuel Macron also pushed a “forward deterrence initiative” earlier this year that could see French nuclear weapons deployed elsewhere in Europe.
Moscow has warned that such a strategy could backfire, saying it cannot “ignore an obvious buildup of the nuclear component of NATO’s joint potential.”
Switzerland, meanwhile, has backed EU sanctions against Russia, prompting Moscow to designate it an “unfriendly nation.” Bern has also considered easing restrictions on the re-export of Swiss-made weapons to Ukraine, sparking criticism from the country’s largest party that its longstanding neutrality is being eroded.
Strikes on Russian infrastructure
The takeover also comes amid continued Ukrainian attacks on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure.
Ukraine has recently targeted warehouses and logistics facilities belonging to Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries, and its rival Ozon. Kiev has acknowledged deliberately striking the facilities, claiming their networks are used by the Russian military to procure, store and transport dual-use goods. Moscow rejects the allegations and has denounced the attacks as terrorism.
Ukrainian media reported in July that French intelligence was providing “critical targeting assistance” for strikes on at least eight Wildberries facilities, as well as refineries and other infrastructure.
How important is Russia to the companies?
Russia has been a significant market for the French retailers. At its peak, Auchan Russia was one of the country’s largest foreign retail chains and was still operating around 230 stores as of 2025. ELO reported in 2023 that Russia generated 10% of its revenue, making it the group’s third-largest market after France and Spain.
ADEO relinquished operational control of its Russian subsidiary in 2023, handing management to local executives. However, documents obtained by French investigative outlet L’Informe indicated that ADEO continued to classify the operation as a subsidiary and an “autonomous business unit.”
Leroy Merlin, rebranded as Lemana PRO in Russia in 2024, remained a major source of revenue for ADEO. L’Informe reported that Russia was the group’s second-largest market by revenue after France in 2024 and accounted for around 18.5% of its worldwide revenue in 2025.
Nestle has less exposure. Its Russian operations account for about 1% of global sales, according to Jean-Philippe Bertschy, an analyst at Swiss investment bank Vontobel. RBK estimated Nestle Russia’s revenue at 258 billion rubles ($3.06 billion) in 2025.
How have the companies reacted?
Auchan and Lemana PRO said they had received no official notification from the Russian authorities about the status of their assets and had requested clarification. Both said their stores were operating normally as of Friday.
Nestle said it “takes note” of the presidential decree and is “assessing the situation and its options.” The company said it would take “all necessary steps to protect its rights and ensure continuity of business operations in the interests of all stakeholders.”
What happens to the assets?
Under the 2023 framework, foreign owners temporarily lose control of assets placed under management but do not automatically forfeit ownership.
Some assets have been transferred directly to Russian state bodies. In 2023, the Russian operations of Germany’s Uniper and Finland’s Fortum were placed under the Federal Property Management Agency.
In other cases, Moscow has authorized sales. Putin approved the sale of Goldman Sachs’ Russian subsidiary to Balchug Capital in January 2025.
The system also allows assets to be returned. In March 2025, Italian appliance maker Ariston regained control of Ariston Thermo Rus after announcing its return to the Russian market. The subsidiary had been placed under the temporary management of Gazprom Household Systems the previous year.
Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said in 2025 that cases would be assessed individually. Companies that left under government pressure but preserved jobs, contacts and technology, as well as a buy-back option, could be allowed to return, he said.

articles.title: Pact with Saudi Arabia threatens to draw Pakistan into Middle East conflict
articles.body:
As he stood in Riyadh last September, the world looked like a very different place for Pakistan’s most powerful man, Gen Asim Munir.
The country’s army chief was there to witness the signing of a historic defence pact with Saudi Arabia, which he had personally orchestrated with the crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman.
To Munir, it appeared to be a highly strategic win: Riyadh would provide cash-strapped Pakistan with billions of dollars of life-saving investments and loans. In exchange, Pakistan agreed to train up the Saudi military, and Pakistan’s armed forces would defend Saudi Arabia in the unlikely event of an attack on its territory.
Analysts say it was clear that Pakistan presumed US-Iran relations would soon get back on track and the risk of a conflict sweeping across the Middle East and the Gulf was low.
But a very different scenario soon unfolded. By February, the Middle East was on fire after the US and Israel began bombing Iran – and Iran began firing missiles at the Gulf states, including Saudi Arabia, in retaliation.
It did not take long for the war to reinflame Saudi’s conflict with the Houthis, the Iran-backed rebel group based in Yemen, and for their fragile truce to collapse. Earlier this month the Houthis made unprecedented territorial gains in Yemen and hit Saudi territory with strikes and drones. Saudi Arabia has responded by pounding Yemen with airstrikes. Some believe a return to full-scale war is on the horizon.
The pressure is now mounting on Pakistan, and particularly Munir. In August, the defence pact with Saudi Arabia was extended to include Turkey and renamed the Mecca joint defence agreement. The countries agreed that an armed attack on any one of them would be treated as an attack on all three.
Ayesha Siddiqa, a defence analyst and senior fellow at King’s College London, said: “I don’t think Asim Munir properly calculated the threats the region was facing – and that Pakistan might need to put its troops on the line quite so soon.”
Saudi Arabia has tens of billions of dollars in fighter jets and war machinery, but it does not have any warfare experience to fight the Houthis, who have proved to be tough, resilient fighters. Pakistan’s forces, trained to deal with the constant menace of India, would be highly valuable on the frontline.
Analysts say that if Saudi Arabia decided to activate the Mecca pact to fight the Houthis, Pakistan would have no choice but to send in its troops, including thousands who are already deployed in Saudi Arabia for training. As well as being a defence partner, Pakistan is almost totally economically and geopolitically dependent on Saudi Arabia, which has recently given the country a lifesaving $8bn (£6bn) in funds and investments.
Last week, Pakistani government ministers and senior military figures gave increasingly bullish statements, confirming their “unconditional” commitment to the pact and saying Islamabad would go to “any extent” to defend Saudi Arabia.
But privately, officials in Pakistan are deeply worried about being dragged into the never-ending war unfolding across the Middle East. The country is already economically crippled, in a de facto war with the Taliban in Afghanistan, and facing an uncontrollable surge in militancy in its border areas.
To many, an activation of the Mecca pact would be perceived as Islamabad taking a clear stance against Iran. Before the US and Israeli strikes on Iran, Pakistan had good relations with its neighbour – ties that Munir utilised to bring Tehran to the negotiating table in his attempt to secure a lasting ceasefire. But as the war has dragged on, Pakistan has become increasingly infuriated with Iran, while Tehran has little trust left in Islamabad.
As Siddiqa emphasised, Pakistan joining the fight against the Houthis “would come with major repercussions”. After Iran, Pakistan is home to the second-largest population of Shia Muslims, who would probably rise up in protest against any involvement in strikes on the Houthis.
Iran also maintains good relations with the Taliban in Afghanistan, posing the risk of further provoking one of Pakistan’s biggest security threats and driving militancy and security problems along the Afghanistan-Pakistan border to even deadlier levels.
It also risks inflaming the situation in Balochistan, Pakistan’s unstable border region with Iran, which is home to a long-running and uncontrollable insurgency.
Raja Nasir Abbas, the opposition leader in Pakistan’s senate, said that only the very few at the top of Pakistan’s military even knew what conditions and agreements had been made in the Mecca pact. With the military as Pakistan’s de facto rulers, the decision to join was not even put before parliament.
“It will be a disaster for the country if Pakistan jumps into war,” said Abbas. “We are already facing two lethal insurgencies; our economy is in a shambles and inflation has rocketed. If we take Saudi Arabia’s side in this conflict, the country will face chaos, instability and religious division.”
So far, no one has been able to pinpoint what the “red line” would be that would force the pact to be activated. Analysts said Pakistan appeared to be banking on Riyadh’s reluctance to enter into open warfare with Iran by escalating its fight with the Houthis. Turkey has also made it clear it does not want to enter the fray.
“Pakistan will do its best not to get involved in any incursion on Yemeni soil,” said Muhammad Amir Rana, the director of the Islamabad-based Pak Institute for Peace Studies.
Speaking privately, one senior official said he did not think the Saudi crown prince “wants to activate the pact now”.
“If the kingdom plans to send its ground forces, Pakistan would support that,” he said. “But I don’t think Saudi Arabia would start a full-fledged war against the Houthis without American approval and Trump has snubbed them. Right now, the US does not want to open up another front; they prefer talking to Houthis.”
He added: “You can’t predict the future though.”

articles.title: Russia Enlists Yemeni Citizens for War in Ukraine, Ukraine Intel Says
articles.body:
The Foreign Intelligence Service of Ukraine (SZRU) has identified at least 27 Yemeni nationals whom Russian authorities intend to deploy in combat operations against Ukraine, according to an intelligence assessment published on Saturday, Sept. 19.
The SZRU stated that Russian military bodies are directly involved in the administrative processing of the recruits, indicating an institutionalized recruitment pipeline designed to channel foreign nationals into active combat units.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to intelligence files, the head of the military contract selection center in Khanty-Mansiysk, identified as Lieutenant Pervushin, submitted a formal request to the Russian border service in July 2026 seeking expedited legal status for a group of Yemeni citizens.
Following their formal entry and residency legalization, Russian defense authorities prepared standard military service contracts for their enlistment.
The intelligence service reported that the identified cohort includes individuals born in 2006 and 2007.
Administrative pipeline
The recruitment mechanism relies on presidential decrees issued by Russian Vladimir Putin that established simplified and expedited pathways for foreign nationals to obtain temporary residence permits and fast-track Russian citizenship in exchange for military service.
The SZRU noted that the administrative scheme functions by first granting foreign recruits legal status inside the Russian Federation under simplified migration rules, after which regional military recruitment centers execute contractual enlistment procedures.
Poland Joins European Coalition on Ballistic Missile Defense
The intelligence agency stated that the use of regional enlistment offices in administrative districts such as the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Okrug reflects continuous efforts by the Russian defense establishment to replenish frontline personnel without declaring an overt nationwide mobilization.
Houthi-linked recruitment networks
The SZRU findings follow previous disclosures regarding Russian recruitment of Yemeni citizens to sustain operations in Ukraine.
In late 2024, reporting by the Financial Times revealed that hundreds of Yemeni nationals had been recruited into the Russian military through commercial entities linked to the Houthi movement in Yemen, specifically Al Jabri General Trading & Investment Co SPC.
Recruits reported being lured to Moscow with promises of high-paying engineering, technical, or security employment alongside fast-track Russian citizenship, only to be forcibly transferred to military bases and compelled to sign Russian-language enlistment contracts under threat.
Regional security analysts noted that economic hardship in Yemen has facilitated recruitment efforts by foreign networks. The personnel transfers coincide with deepening coordination between Moscow and Iranian-backed regional groups, including high-level bilateral talks regarding potential transfers of Russian defense hardware, such as P-800 Oniks anti-ship cruise missiles, to Houthi forces.

articles.title: Defender Media: Ukraine’s battle-tested drone makers reach no top slot in Pentagon’s $1.1 billion Drone Dominance program, but some Ukrainian technology wins anyway
articles.body:
Ukraine's battle-tested drone makers did not win a single top slot in the Pentagon's latest drone contest. But some Ukrainian technology won anyway, competing quietly under the names of Western partners, The Defender Media reports.
The Pentagon's $1.1 billion Drone Dominance program does not allow direct purchases from Ukrainian firms, which must set up a US legal entity to bid.
The Ukrainians who competed under their own names were hampered by export licenses, the hunt for non-Chinese components, and visa issues, and none of the four cracked the top five in either category.
American firms sweep the top slots
The Pentagon picked five winners each in two categories, long-range strikes out to 15 kilometers and close-in assault. Eric Schmidt's Perennial Autonomy topped the long-range field with its Hornet drone, on 80.1 points, and Neros led the close-in category with 88.1. Neros already supplies Ukraine with 6,000 of its Archer FPV drones.
The rest of the winners, from ORQA's US arm to XTEND and ModalAI, were American as well. All will receive Pentagon supply contracts, with order sizes to be set later.
Ukrainians win under other flags
The Ukrainian firms that announced their entries, F-Drones, General Chereshnya, Grim Tech, and Stellarion, all missed the cut, though General Chereshnya had reached the program's second round earlier in the year.
Bureaucracy tripped the open entrants
Stellarion laid out what went wrong. Getting export permits and moving hardware took so long that integrating American parts, including warheads, and adapting the finished system on schedule became "complicated," its representatives said.
Finding NDAA-compliant, non-Chinese components ate up more time, and visa delays kept its specialists from fixing technical problems on site.
Firms that missed the top five can enter later rounds: a Gauntlet 2.5 contest for bomber drones is set for October, and a third phase begins in February 2027, with missions built to test control of several drones at once.
