articles.title: Democratic Leaders Fear the New Russia Sanctions Bill Could 'Harm' Americans. Here's Why
articles.body:
President Donald Trump on Friday signed a sweeping Russia sanctions bill intended to target the country's financial institutions and the energy industry, which has largely financed the assault on Ukraine.
The legislation, which also extends sanctions on Iran's energy and weapons sectors, has been hailed for its harsher measures on Russia, with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky calling it “an extremely powerful tool.” However, Democratic leaders have expressed grave concern over the broader tariff authority it affords to Trump.
The new law allows Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on countries that make “new purchases of crude oil or natural gas” originating from Russia, or any country among the top five importers of Russian oil or gas over the last 12 months.
According to the Center for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), the top three purchasers of Russian oil and gas in August were China, India, and Turkey.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, says Trump’s previous ambition to introduce tariffs using any available avenue has ignited the concern among Democrats.
“The reason why people are so nervous about this is that the authority is extremely wide, and has been handed to an Administration that has already shown great latitude to follow the spirit of the law,” Elms tells TIME. “Tariffs could be set at 100%. It's really at the discretion of the Executive Branch.”
Democratic leaders sound the alarm on “terribly flawed” bill
The House passed the bill with bipartisan support on Wednesday. The Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, named in honor of the late Republican Senator who spent the final year of his life building support for the measure, passed with 262 votes to 159. Some 58 Democrats voted with the majority of Republicans in favor of the bill, despite objections from party leadership.
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries led the Democratic opposition to the bill, raising concerns over extending Trump new tariff powers that he said could "give the President an additional tool to visit economic harm on the American people."
“Why in the world would this Congress or the People's House give this President unfettered authority to visit more tariffs on the world that will have an adverse economic impact on the American people?” the New York Representative questioned ahead of the vote.
After the bill passed, Jeffries told TIME that Trump “cannot be entrusted with new powers to impose tariffs that will further raise costs for American families.”
TIME has reached out to the White House for comment.
Shortly after his return to office, Trump implemented global tariffs as part of what he called a “Liberation Day.” Although the majority of those were shut down by a Supreme Court ruling in February that deemed them illegal, his general use—and threatened use—of tariffs has continued to fuel international tensions.
Tariffs introduced since Trump’s return have already made their mark on American households, experts say. The Yale Budget Lab in late August estimated that household costs due to tariffs “total about $1,100 annually under current law.”
The U.S.-Canada has raised fresh concerns over the financial impact on American consumers.
Many Americans are already struggling with the cost of living crisis. The Urban Institute in April found that “49% of people in American families don’t have the resources to cover essential expenses to live securely in their community.”
Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, the top Democrat on the Foreign Affairs Committee, has also raised concerns about the potential impact on American families.
In the weeks leading up to the Russia sanctions bill, he urged lawmakers to find a “compromise that properly punishes Russia for its illegal war of aggression against the Ukrainian people, while protecting the American people from reckless inflationary tariffs.”
In a statement to TIME after the vote, Meeks said he found it "regrettable" that lawmakers chose not to “place more guardrails” on the bill’s tariff authorities.
Similar concerns were raised by Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia, who described the bill as “well intentioned, but terribly flawed” in its efforts to hinder Russia’s war effort against Ukraine. “Trump has abused every tariff authority Congress has delegated to the President,” Beyer told TIME, accusing his colleagues of choosing to “ignore our warnings that he is highly likely to continue that pattern with this bill.”
Beyer had delivered a stark warning on the floor ahead of the vote, insisting the bill “would do more harm than good for America and for Ukraine.”
“Trump has abused every presidential tariff authority—every single one—that Congress has given, often to target our allies. This bill has a loophole that would allow him to define basically any country as a facilitator of evading Russian sanctions,” he argued. “He could then hit them with tariffs of up to 100%, with no guardrails or oversight, and no expiration. It’s a much stronger tariff power than those he has already abused, and it would be much harder to challenge in court. Giving him this power when he has shown us over and over again what he will do with it would be an incredible mistake.”
Why other Democratic lawmakers supported the legislation
The legislation’s capacity to economically isolate Russia earned it the bipartisan support needed to get the bill to Trump’s desk.
The bill allows for the further introduction of sanctions on persons and financial institutions affiliated with the Russian government, the prohibiting of energy exports and investment into Russia, and blocks the transfer of funds to the Kremlin.
The bill also includes the potential to expand sanctions on Iran, and comes amid growing concerns from the U.S. over the relationship between Moscow and Tehran. The U.S. Treasury on Monday announced the latest sanctions targeting the Russian bank VTB over allegations it is involved “in Iranian sanctions evasion.”
Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur of Ohio, who co-chairs and co-founded the Congressional Ukraine Caucus, is in firm favor of the legislation. ”We're going to pay close attention to the Administration and to see what they're going to do with these new powers that have been given,” she told TIME after the vote.
Kaptur previously said that both the sanctions and tariff measures were “the best chance we have to get bipartisan legislation signed into law to hold Russia accountable and achieve peace.”
Rep. Steny Hoyer of Maryland also praised the legislation, championing it as an additional way to showcase support for Kyiv. “Today we took a step to redeem our pledge to Ukraine, to support their sovereignty and their democracy,” said Hoyer outside the Capitol. “We will sanction, actively and effectively, Russian criminal behavior.”
How China and India could be impacted by the Russia sanctions bill
The legislation extends Trump the authority to impose tariffs on new and prominent importers of Russian oil and gas.
The legislation could prompt a new wave of tariffs handed out by the President, experts warn. "The tariffs can be introduced across the board," says Elms. “This is what makes it so alarming.”
China and India are two major importers of Russian oil and gas and therefore stand to be the most affected. In August, China was importing roughly 1.25 million barrels of Russian Crude oil daily, according to commodity analysts Kpler via Reuters. India imported record-highs of 2.5 million barrels daily of Russian Crude in June, per Kpler's analysis.
According to The European External Action Service (EEAS), Russia’s shadow fleet—largely unregulated oil tankers transiting sanctioned oil—includes between 600 to 1,400 vessels. Exports are crucial for China and India, the leading importers of seaborne oil from Russia.
U.S. sanctions have already targeted Russian oil tankers and Moscow’s energy industry in response to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Still, China and India have remained steady buyers, but the threat of tariffs could change the attitude of both countries, experts predict.
“I think they will be quite concerned on this one,” says Elms. “Presumably because of this [bill], we will see some diversification away from Russian energy by India and China.”
While the Supreme Court ruling barring most of Trump’s prior tariffs cited Congressional power to impose tariffs, this argument won’t be applicable if lawmakers attempt to restrict the President’s ability. “In this case, Congress has quite clearly given that authority to the President,” says Elms.
Beijing has hit back firmly against the tariff measures included in the bill. “China opposes long-arm jurisdiction and unilateral sanctions that have no basis in international law,” said Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun.
The legislation comes at a crucial time for U.S.-China relations, just a week ahead of President Xi Jinping’s visit to Washington. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is also set to meet with his Chinese counterpart, Vice Premier He Lifeng, this weekend.
The U.S. already has a number of tariffs in place on Chinese goods, including a tariff of up to 12.5% on goods allegedly made with forced labor. The U.S. Trade Representative's last year launched a tariff investigation into China's "apparent failure" to comply with the "Phase One" trade deal signed with Trump in 2020.
Meanwhile, India’s Foreign Ministry responded to the new sanctions bill by saying it was “monitoring further developments." The statement said India "remains firmly committed to ensuring energy security for its 1.4 billion people" and "will continue to do so through diversified sourcing."
The statement said imports of Russian energy had been discussed with U.S. officials in recent months, and that “implications for not just the bilateral relationship, but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.”
Trump threatened tariffs on Indian goods last August in response to Delhi’s continued purchasing of Russian oil. “They don’t care how many people in Ukraine are being killed by the Russian war machine,” claimed Trump, days ahead of his meeting with President Vladimir Putin that yielded no concrete results.
Similar to China, India also currently faces a tariff on alleged forced labor goods, with the levy landing at 10%.
After agreeing on a framework for a bilateral trade agreement in February, Delhi and Washington have continued negotiations since.
“India and the U.S. have been supposedly a ‘moment away’ from a bilateral agreement,” says Elms. “I think it is highly unlikely now that India will actually sign that agreement because they are now potentially subject to new tariffs at any time.”

articles.title: Ukraine’s Vivaldi operation cleared 85 square kilometers near Lyman. A soldier who fought it says one thing was hardest of all
articles.body:
A soldier of Artan, a special unit of Ukraine's Defense Intelligence, known by the callsign Derun, described the fighting during important Ukraine's Operation Vivaldi, according to Novyny.Live. He says the hardest part of Ukraine's counteroffensive in the northern part of Donetsk Oblast is prying Russian troops out of positions they have fortified so well that they see every approach coming.
Vivaldi is bigger than any one assault. It is the counteroffensive that the Third Army Corps is running near Lyman. The Institute for the Study of War says it has disrupted Russia's plan to encircle the fortified "Fortress Belt" of Donetsk cities, as the corps says its first phase cleared 75 square kilometers of Russian infiltrators and de-occupied another 10.
Dug-in Russians see every approach
The problem is Russia's preparation, when "the enemy has made his positions very well fortified," Derun said.
"The hardest is to knock him out of there, because when a position is competently prepared, they see everything," he explained.
A well-sited position lets the defenders watch the open ground an assault group has to cross, spot the attackers early, and fight them at a distance, which is the worst way for the attacker to come.
A lapse opens the way in
When Russian troops stop watching the approaches to their position, the assault group can close the gap unseen, Derun said.
"When Russian troops are distracted, it can play into our hands: we can approach under cover, when he does not see us, and work him from close range," he added.
Once the attackers are in close, he added, the defenders can start to panic and make mistakes.
Vivaldi runs to four seasons
Artan fought as part of a larger force. Alongside the Third Army Corps' own brigades, the operation drew in Ukraine's Special Operations Forces, the border guard, and the military-intelligence unit, all under a single tactical command, and it ran for months under an information blackout before the corps disclosed it.
The corps commander, Andrii Biletskyi, said the phase revealed so far is only the first of four, naming the operation for Vivaldi's Four Seasons.
"This is only the first," he said, promising more.

articles.title: UK military sites see near-daily drone incidents in 2026 as Europe confronts widening hybrid threat
articles.body:
UK military sites see near-daily drone incidents in 2026 as Europe confronts widening hybrid threat
Close to 340 drone incidents were recorded at or near U.K. Defense Ministry facilities over the past year, according to newly released figures from the Independent.
The report comes as European governments increasingly warn of growing hybrid warfare threats from Russia, while suspicious drone activity disrupts infrastructure across the continent.
The 340 incidents were recorded in 2026 over eight months through August, according to data obtained under freedom-of-information laws and reported by the Independent. With drone incidents occurring at a near-daily rate, the 2026 total could climb significantly higher by the end of the year.
By August, U.K. drone incidents had already surpassed the 250 recorded during all of 2025 and 126 in 2024.
The U.K. Defense Ministry has not publicly stated who it suspects is behind the incidents, but experts cited in the report pointed to actors working in the interests of Russia or Iran.
Former U.K. Defense Minister Tobias Ellwood said the rise suggests British forces are increasingly being treated "as a target." He criticized what he said were inadequate protections around military and critical infrastructure, accusing the government of being "asleep."
Drone flights over the U.K. are part of widespread UAV activity across Europe. As the Independent released its figures on drone incursions near military installations, Luxembourg's Findel airport temporarily halted operations on Sept. 18 after suspected drone activity near the airport.
The unexplained drone activity comes as NATO officials warn that hybrid attacks are increasingly aimed at undermining public confidence and cohesion within the alliance.
Speaking at a NATO press conference in Copenhagen on Sept. 19, Military Committee Chair Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone said the alliance must balance deterrence with avoiding escalation.
"Escalation management is part of our mindset, of our attitude," Dragone said, adding that NATO also needs to "send a message of strength."
Dragone said public opinion itself has become a target of hybrid activity, with the goal of creating distrust in political leaders and disrupting alliance unity.
European governments are stepping up preparations for possible Russian hybrid attacks as officials across the continent warn that Moscow could increasingly use drones, missiles, sabotage, and cyberattacks to test NATO countries and pressure them over their support for Ukraine.

Russian President Vladimir Putin claimed that Ukraine is unwilling to engage in genuine peace negotiations, asserting that Kyiv is actively taking steps to prevent a diplomatic resolution to the war.
Addressing a meeting of Russia’s Military-Industrial Commission on Friday, Sept. 18, Putin alleged that Ukrainian calls for diplomatic engagement are disingenuous, state news agency Interfax reported.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Representatives of the Kyiv regime, the leadership in Kyiv, speak of peace and propose resuming so-called negotiations, but themselves commit such crimes, doing everything to ensure that there is no peace and no negotiations,” Putin claimed.
The Russian leader contended that Moscow cannot be intimidated and insisted that recent Ukrainian actions demonstrate a refusal to negotiate. His remarks follow a series of Ukrainian drone strikes on defense-industrial and refining facilities across western and central Russia, as well as recurring cross-border engagements.
Despite the Kremlin’s accusations, Ukrainian officials have repeatedly presented diplomatic initiatives to end hostilities, including proposals for an unconditional ceasefire and direct leader-level talks.
However, Moscow has consistently conditioned any diplomatic engagement on sweeping political concessions, including international recognition of its illegal annexations and Kyiv ceding control of remaining areas in the Donbas.
US Approves $2.68B Air Defense Equipment Sale to Ukraine
Putin’s true goal
Putin’s assertions contrast with assessments delivered earlier in the week by President Volodymyr Zelensky, who warned that the Kremlin leader remains fundamentally committed to destroying Ukrainian sovereignty rather than settling a localized territorial dispute.
Zelensky stated that Putin’s ambition extends far beyond consolidating occupied frontline territory.
“The problem is that we have to change Putin’s mind,” Zelensky said, responding to US mediation concepts focused on drawing new territorial borders. “He needs Ukraine. He needs Ukraine to be a part of Russia.”
Zelensky emphasized that Kyiv remains prepared for an unconditional cessation of hostilities if Moscow halts combat operations along the existing line of contact, allowing international mediators to facilitate diplomatic talks.
However, he firmly dismissed the concept of a “win-win” compromise promoted by external mediators, arguing that an unprovoked war that has claimed hundreds of thousands of lives cannot yield mutual benefit.
The president reaffirmed his readiness to meet Putin directly if such an encounter could produce concrete progress toward a lasting peace, while reiterating that robust Western security guarantees remain essential to prevent Russia from using an operational pause to prepare future offensives.
Washington weighs pre-settlement economic incentives
The diplomatic impasse arrives amid reports that the administration of US President Donald Trump is exploring preliminary commercial agreements with Moscow before achieving a definitive peace settlement.
Washington is assessing whether concluding bilateral economic deals could signal seriousness regarding a long-term diplomatic reset and incentivize Russian elites to support ending the war. A US official told the newspaper that business agreements could help persuade hardline figures surrounding Putin that Washington seeks a constructive bilateral framework.
The prospective approach would mark a shift from previous US policy, which insisted that commercial ties and economic normalization could occur only after Russia ends its military aggression against Ukraine. Potential areas of cooperation previously raised by Moscow and Washington have encompassed energy partnerships, critical mineral investments, Arctic transit routes, and corporate joint ventures.
During early September discussions in Moscow between Putin and US special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov confirmed that talks addressed potential large-scale, mutually beneficial commercial projects alongside conflict settlement concepts.

articles.title: U.S. approves Ukraine air defense package with unclear weapons
articles.body:
- The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.68 billion air defense sale to Ukraine on Sept. 18, funded through European contributions and prior U.S. military financing.
- The package lists "S-300 Clone" and "GAM-67" missiles, designations that don't match any publicly known current weapon system.
The U.S. State Department approved a possible $2.68 billion sale of air defense equipment to Ukraine on Sept. 18, a package built around several weapons whose exact identity the notification itself does not make clear.
The Defense Security Cooperation Agency’s notification to Congress describes the deal as an “Air Defense Development Upgrade.” Ukraine would pay for it through a mix of European contributions and U.S. Foreign Military Financing that Congress appropriated under the prior administration, with that American funding counted as a one-to-one capital contribution to the Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund. The sale still needs to clear the standard congressional review period before any contract can be finalized, and the eventual contractors would be chosen through a competitive U.S. government procurement process.
The equipment list includes items called S-300 Clone missiles and GAM-67 missiles, along with Range-Extended Air Defense Laser Guided Rocket missile systems, a launcher platform called the Improvised Transporter Erector Launcher 1.5, mobile launcher modification kits, and RPS 202 counter-drone radars, plus the usual mix of spare parts, software, training publications and logistics support that accompanies most Foreign Military Sales packages.
Two of those names don’t match any publicly known current weapon system. GAM-67 is the U.S. Air Force’s old designation for the Crossbow, a turbojet-powered anti-radar missile program that Northrop’s Ventura Division built in the 1950s. Only 14 were ever produced, and the Air Force canceled the program in 1957 because the missile was too slow to be useful against modern air defenses. That history makes it clear the notification isn’t describing a Cold War-era leftover; the designation appears to have been reused, whether as a placeholder or a formal label for something new, rather than referring to the original Crossbow. “S-300 Clone” is similarly undefined in any public Pentagon or industry documentation, and no other name for it has surfaced.
The most plausible explanation available comes from outside the official notification. Robert Hamilton, a retired U.S. Army colonel who now leads the Delphi Global Research Center, told PBS NewsHour that the United States and Ukraine have been working jointly either to modernize Ukraine’s aging stock of S-300 interceptor missiles or to develop a newer version of the missile with improved capability. Hamilton said he expects that upgraded system to become operational close to the end of 2026. Neither the State Department nor Ukraine’s government has confirmed that this effort is the same program referenced as “S-300 Clone” in Friday’s notification, but the timing and subject matter line up closely enough that the two appear connected.
The S-300 is a Soviet-designed, long-range surface-to-air missile system that Ukraine inherited in large numbers and has relied on throughout the war, alongside Western systems like the Patriot. Ukraine has faced a persistent shortage of S-300 interceptors because Russia is now the only producer of the original missile, making any American-backed alternative, cloned, modernized or newly built, a potentially significant addition to Ukraine’s ability to keep those launchers firing.
The State Department’s notification includes the standard language used in nearly all such filings: the sale would not require additional U.S. government or contractor personnel in Ukraine, would not affect U.S. military readiness, and would not alter the basic military balance in the region. No offset agreement has been proposed so far; any such arrangement would be negotiated separately between Ukraine and whichever companies win the eventual contracts.
What remains unclear is what the S-300 Clone and GAM-67 items actually are, technically or physically. Congress has not yet completed its review, and neither Washington nor Kyiv has released further detail on the specifications, quantities, or delivery timeline for either item.

articles.title: No meeting can force Iran to surrender
articles.body:
No meeting can force Iran to surrender
Siasat-e-Rooz examined the meeting of senior military commanders from the United States, Israel, and several Arab countries in Germany, writing that Arab states are currently facing a major crisis: the collapse of their security-building strategy based on US presence and, in some cases, normalization with Israel.
This reality became clear not only during the Ramadan War but also in recent developments in Yemen. Although these states have previously formed coalitions with the US, making this nothing new, the key point is that the Berlin meeting will ultimately not change regional equations. Such a gathering will neither improve regional security nor reduce tensions; instead, it will intensify them and further contribute to the tightening of the Strait of Hormuz. Arab countries that rejected the Oman meeting cannot now expect the Berlin meeting to force Iran to surrender or reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Therefore, before becoming trapped in a difficult situation, they should abandon the illusion of an American security umbrella and take steps toward localized security alongside Iran.
Shargh: Why has China entered the Hormuz file?
Shargh evaluated the importance of the Strait of Hormuz for China. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi considers reopening the Strait of Hormuz essential for stabilizing energy transport and preventing the crisis from spreading to Yemen and the Red Sea. Beijing’s motivation is not merely political. China has long been the largest buyer of Iranian oil, and any disruption in Persian Gulf energy exports directly affects its economy. Thus, when Wang Yi speaks about reopening Hormuz, there is a clear economic and security concern behind his position. Attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure and pressure on the Bab al-Mandab route have expanded the crisis from a single strait to a network of vital energy corridors. As a result, Beijing can no longer treat Hormuz as merely an Iran–US issue; each day of continued crisis makes the energy and trade implications more serious for China.
Hamshahri: The map of Middle East trade routes
Hamshahri wrote that disruptions in shipping caused by the Iran–US war have pushed Middle East countries toward roads, railways, pipelines, and even new fiber‑optic routes, reshaping the region’s trade map. The war has challenged the region’s historic dependence on maritime routes. Disruptions in ship traffic through Hormuz have ushered in a new phase of regional trade—one in which roads, railways, land borders, pipelines, and even alternative sea routes have become core elements of economic security. At the same time, recent events—such as the attack on Saudi Arabia’s East–West pipeline—show that even alternative oil routes are not immune to war. Thus, the issue is not simply replacing Hormuz; the conflict is exposing the vulnerability of an entire chain of regional corridors. The new transformation in the Middle East is therefore not just the revival of land routes but a simultaneous competition and reconfiguration among multiple trade and energy corridors.
Sazandegi: The JCPOA is still alive
Sazandegi analyzed Thursday night’s event at the UN Security Council, where China and Russia vetoed the US draft resolution against Iran. The incident shows the JCPOA can still influence Iran’s legal and political dynamics. Russia and China vetoed the US resolution to extend the mandate of the Iran sanctions expert panel by citing the very clause in the JCPOA and Resolution 2231 that outlines the termination of Iran’s file at the Security Council. For this reason, the Islamabad understanding should be taken more seriously, and efforts should be made to implement it. The issue is not merely the text of an Iran–US understanding; it is about creating a pathway for resolving disputes—especially given that both countries have experienced the costly consequences of withdrawing from agreements and returning to confrontation. The veto by Russia and China once again revealed the divide among permanent Security Council members over the legacy of the 2015 nuclear deal.
Farhikhtegan: Why BRICS matters for Iran
The composition of BRICS shows clearly that it is not a unified bloc. Russia, facing Western sanctions, has adopted firmer positions toward the West. China seeks to avoid confrontation, and India does not want BRICS to be defined as anti‑Western. Nevertheless, a large portion of Iran’s economy depends on interactions with BRICS members. China, the UAE, India, Brazil, and Russia are among Iran’s main partners—and all are BRICS members. Emphasizing national currencies and creating alternatives to SWIFT can reduce much of the impact of unilateral sanctions. Beyond economics, the West has tried for at least two decades to isolate Iran diplomatically, but BRICS membership has undermined that strategy. Another reason BRICS is important is its ability to prevent anti‑Iran statements: since Iran is a member and final communiqués require unanimous approval, no anti‑Iran statement will be issued within BRICS.

articles.title: What are “S-300 Clone” and GAM-67 in America’s new $2.68 billion package for Ukraine? Experts think they have answer
articles.body:
The US is preparing to sell Ukraine something unusual: American-made missiles for its Soviet S-300 air-defense systems. The missiles, labeled "S-300 Clone" in the paperwork, are part of a $2.68 billion package that the State Department approved on 18 September, financed by European partners and unused US military aid, Defense Express reports.
Ukraine has plenty of Soviet-era S-300 launchers but not the missiles to feed them. Russia will not sell more, and an earlier Ukrainian attempt to build its own went nowhere, according to Defense Mirror.
Not a Soviet 5V55 replica
At the same time, the missile itself is not actually a "clone" or replica of the Soviet 5V55. According to Defense Express's own information, this is a new development with enhanced characteristics and a different, more modern targeting guidance principle.
At the same time, the American side did not disclose the index, characteristics, or manufacturer of the missiles mentioned in the State Department's statement.

articles.title: South Korea rejects US pressure for deployments to Hormuz
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
South Korea rejects US pressure for deployments to Hormuz
South Korea is rejecting pressure from the US to deploy its navy to the Strait of Hormuz, with President Lee Jae Myung saying on Friday he would not involve his country in the ongoing US-Iran war.
"There won't be [a] deployment that would involve or enter war. I can tell you that very clearly," he told a press conference, adding that "we won't deploy military assets in any form to that end".
Lee did caveat the comments, saying that South Korea was reviewing playing a role in ensuring free navigation in the region.
"[It] is also clear we must do the minimum as other countries do to protect our commercial shipping and crude shipments, and also the safety of our people," he said.
Lee's comments come as commercial shipping around the Middle East, specifically in the Gulf and Red Sea, comes under increasing strain from both Iran and the Houthis as a means of exerting pressure on the global economy in response to the U/S-Israeli war launched in February.
This has directly affected South Korea, which imported 70% of its oil from the Gulf prior to the outbreak of the war, alongside significant portions of LNG.
It also comes amid threats from US President Donald Trump, who asked the country in August to "give us a hand" with Iran, later saying he would scale back military drills after South Korea said no.
He also questioned why South Korea would say no, given that tens of thousands of US troops are stationed in the country.
"We have 39,000 soldiers over there guarding you from Kim Jong-un, your next-door neighbour. And you're not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran? That’s strange," he said.
Trump and members of his administration have also criticised European allies for not getting involved in the war.
The US has 28,500 troops stationed in South Korea, one of the longest continuous US military deployments, having been there since 1957.
Since the start of the war, the US has redeployed some forces out of the country, most importantly Patriot and THAAD batteries needed to intercept Iranian ballistic missiles.
Alongside Lee's comments, South Korean Foreign Minister Cho Hyun met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
South Korea's foreign ministry said that Cho had explained to Rubio that the country would make a contribution to restoring freedom of navigation, though it didn't elaborate what this would look like.

articles.title: Trump Signs Russia-Iran Sanctions Bill, Putting New Pressure Tools At His Disposal
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump signed into law legislation aimed at increasing economic pressure on Russia over its war on Ukraine, including by targeting Moscow's energy revenues as well as countries that continue to buy Russian oil and gas.
The White House said on September 18 that Trump signed H.R. 5334, the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 -- the legislation named after the late South Carolina senator who championed tougher measures against Moscow.
The signing makes the Russia sanctions measure law after it passed the Senate by an 86-11 vote in August and the House of Representatives by 262-159 on September 16.
The law gives the Trump administration sweeping new authority to impose sanctions and tariffs on Russia, its energy sector, and foreign governments and entities that help Moscow evade existing restrictions.
But much of its practical impact will depend on decisions by Trump and his administration.
Targeting Russian Energy Revenues, Sanctions Evasion
Among its most consequential provisions, the law authorizes the president to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on goods imported from countries that fall within specified categories tied to purchases of Russian oil and natural gas or the circumvention of US sanctions.
The legislation focuses in particular on five importers of Russian crude oil or natural gas, which purchased the largest amounts of these commodities during the 12-month period preceding its enactment, as well as countries identified as major facilitators of Russian sanctions evasion.
The administration is required to reassess the countries covered by the provisions every 180 days.
The law also targets Russia's so-called shadow fleet -- the vessels and networks used to transport Russian energy and evade sanctions -- as well as foreign individuals and companies involved in supporting Russian energy production or sanctions evasion. The legislation can affect vessel owners, operators, managers, insurers, and other participants in activities within its scope.
The measure also contains provisions targeting major Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) projects, including Yamal LNG and Arctic LNG 2, large facilities in the Russian Arctic designed to produce and export the fuel.
At the same time, the law gives Trump considerable discretion over how and whether some of its powers are used. He can waive sanctions, restrictions, or duties if he determines that doing so is in the national interest and provides Congress with an explanation.
That means the signing itself does not automatically impose a 100 percent tariff on countries such as China or India. Rather, it gives the administration the statutory authority to impose such duties under specified circumstances.
The legislation also extends the Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 through 2031.
Experts: Implementation Will Determine Impact
Daniel Fried, a former State Department sanctions coordinator, told RFE/RL on September 18 that Trump's decision to sign the measure was significant, but said the president had missed an opportunity to publicly use the moment to send a message to Moscow.
“It’s good that President Trump signed the bill into law,” Fried said. “But the lack of a public statement means that he has missed a chance to send a message to Putin that he needs to end the war.”
Luke Coffey, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute who focuses on national security and transatlantic relations, said the legislation's symbolism was particularly important.
“One of the most important aspects of this new legislation is its symbolism and timing,” Coffey told RFE/RL.
He said the bipartisan support for the measure highlighted the role of Republicans in Congress, including lawmakers who had previously been skeptical about continued US involvement in Ukraine.
Coffey said he hoped the legislation could influence the debate among supporters of the Trump movement by demonstrating how support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia could be framed as being in US interests.
But he cautioned against expecting an immediate wave of new sanctions or tariffs.
“I would not expect major new sanctions or tariffs to be implemented overnight as a result of this legislation,” Coffey said.
Instead, he noted, the law codifies many existing sanctions, which he described as significant in itself.
Coffey also pointed to a provision that has received less attention: a restriction on US businesses pursuing new business deals or investments in Russia, or with Russian entities, until there is a peace agreement acceptable to Ukraine.
He said that provision could become particularly important because some political and business interests in Washington are waiting for an opportunity to restore commercial ties with Moscow.
Kerri Bitsoff, a former senior Treasury Department official who worked at the Office of Foreign Assets Control, said the bipartisan vote was an encouraging signal for Ukraine and demonstrated continued congressional support for maintaining pressure on Russian President Vladimir Putin.
“The bipartisan vote is an encouraging signal for Ukraine, and it shows our Congress still backs pressure on Putin across party lines,” Bitsoff told RFE/RL.
Tariffs have proved difficult to use against major purchasers of Russian energy, she cautioned.
She pointed to China's response to US tariffs in April 2025, when Beijing retaliated with tariffs of its own and restricted rare-earth exports.
“It will take resolve from the president and the American public to stick to the threat,” Bitsoff said.
She also pointed to the enforcement of sanctions already on the books as a key test of how the administration will use the new powers.
“There hasn't been movement from Treasury on the Russia sanctions already in place in almost eleven months,” she said. “Enforcement on those from Treasury will be a good indication of whether Trump will use this new authority or let it sit.”
Zelenskyy Welcomes Trump's Signature
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked Trump and members of Congress for backing the legislation, while invoking Graham's longstanding advocacy for maintaining pressure on Moscow.
“When Lindsey Graham was here in Ukraine, he would always talk about how important it was not to ease pressure on Russia, to strengthen sanctions, and seek a path to peace,” Zelenskyy said in a post to X.
He urged the administration to implement its provisions “fully and swiftly.”
“Peace comes through strength,” Zelenskyy said. “Calm comes through security. And the best guarantee of security is resolve.”

Germany must mobilize its entire society, industry, and armed forces to prepare for national defense and the potential risk of war, according to Inspector General of the Bundeswehr Carsten Breuer, Bild reports on September 17.
Speaking at the IISS Prague Defense Summit, Germany's highest-ranking military officer emphasized that military strength and modern technology alone cannot protect the country against current security challenges.

Breuer noted that rapid technological advances cause military tactics to quickly become outdated. Because of this, according to Bild, he stated that Germany needs to closely study the combat experiences gained during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Russia learns. They copy and adapt, introducing innovations aimed at our strengths and bypassing them. Technology should not determine what we do. We must determine what we do with technology," the general stated.
He stressed that standing up to hybrid threats requires a broader response beyond the capabilities of the armed forces.
Addressing the German people, Breuer said, "Without you, we soldiers are doomed to fail. But failure is not an option. Because that would mean a fatal threat to our societies as we know them. We are all in the same boat."
Breuer had previously ordered the Bundeswehr to achieve full operational capability by 2029 to counter a potential Russian attack on NATO territory.
Funded through an easing of Germany’s constitutional debt brake, the directive prioritizes expanding air defenses, long-range precision strike capabilities, electronic warfare, and ammunition stockpiles following warnings that Russia could rebuild its forces to launch large-scale aggression by 2029.

articles.title: First new British warhead since the early nineties advances
articles.body:
The Astraea programme passed its System Design Review in August 2025, a step the Ministry of Defence describes as significant for the design, safety, performance assessment and manufacturability of what will be the first new British nuclear warhead since the early 1990s, according to the Defence Nuclear Enterprise annual update to Parliament.
The government has committed £15 billion from 2025/26 to 2029/30 to the warhead programme, which includes development of Astraea.
The update states that Astraea “will be the first new UK warhead since the Mk4 warhead (subsequently upgraded to Mk4A) entered service in the early 1990s, and the first to be designed in the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT) era without explosive nuclear testing”.
Designing a warhead without the ability to test it is the central technical challenge of the programme, and the update lists the capabilities delivery depends on, covering products and technology, advanced manufacturing, warhead physics, materials, mission effectiveness, hardness and vulnerability, scientific computing, radiation protection and regulatory science, and criticality safety and non-destructive assay.
AWE is to publish an updated warhead science, engineering and technology strategy this year, compliant with the test ban treaty.
The organisation designs, manufactures and maintains British nuclear warheads, was brought back into government ownership in 2021 and marked its 75th anniversary in 2025. The update says it is undergoing a transformation including major recapitalisation of its infrastructure and nationwide investment across its supply chain and its science, engineering and technology base.
The current warhead remains the Mk4A, fitted to Trident missiles and maintained by AWE at Aldermaston, with the design sovereign to Britain. AWE assures the effectiveness and performance of the warheads along with the safety and security of the stockpile.
The update describes delivery of Astraea as a national endeavour drawing on expertise across government, industry, academia and international partners, with sovereign capability enhanced by partnerships with the United States under the Mutual Defence Agreement and the Polaris Sales Agreement.
The Mutual Defence Agreement, extended indefinitely in 2024, enables cooperation between the two countries on atomic energy for mutual defence purposes, including the exchange of nuclear materials and technology, the transfer of non-nuclear components and collaborative scientific exchanges on technology and nuclear threat reduction.
The missiles the warhead sits on are American built, with Trident and its supporting systems manufactured in the United States, with Britain having bought title to a number drawn from a shared pool of assets under the 1963 Polaris Sales Agreement as amended for Trident in 1982, and the system is operated independently by both the Royal Navy and the United States Navy.

Drones have reportedly appeared near UK Ministry of Defence sites almost daily over past year
The Independent has reported that unidentified drones have appeared near UK Ministry of Defence sites almost every day, leaving the country vulnerable to growing threats from Russia and Iran.
Source: The Independent, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The Independent said, citing data obtained under freedom of information laws, that around 340 drone-related incidents had been recorded at or near Ministry of Defence sites in the year to August 2026. A total of 250 incidents were recorded in 2025, twice the 126 reported the previous year.

Experts, however, said hostile actors working in the interests of Moscow or Tehran are the most obvious suspects. The figures, obtained under freedom of information laws, emerged as Poland warned that the Kremlin leader is planning a drone attack on a NATO member state.
Former Tory defence minister and former Army captain Tobias Ellwood said the sharp rise in drone incidents detected in the UK suggests that the UK Armed Forces are being viewed "as a target". He added that the government is "asleep" to such threats.
Quote from Ellwood: "Here in the UK we are doing nothing about protecting our critical national infrastructure, as well as military bases, and it's such an easy way to disrupt.
At the moment these are just rogue drones, and they're passive, but it's not a huge step to then add a kinetic dimension to them to make them introduce lethality. All this points to the fact that we are not taking the rise in threat levels that our European cousins are addressing seriously at all."

articles.title: Moscow summons British envoy over weapons supplies to Ukraine
articles.body:
The Russian Foreign Ministry summoned Britain's chargé d'affaires in Moscow, Danae Dholakia, on Friday to issue a formal protest about what it called London's "further increase" in weapons supplies to Ukraine.
In a statement, the ministry said that by sending more arms to Kyiv, "London is placing itself in the position of an accomplice to the bloody atrocities committed by the Kyiv regime, which can only be characterized as terrorism and war crimes."
A spokesperson for Britain's Foreign Office called the summoning "yet another attempt to deflect attention from Russia's barbaric full-scale invasion of Ukraine and discredit the UK on the world stage."
Russia currently has no ambassador in London, and relations are dire.
The departure of the previous Russian ambassador, Andrei Kelin, in July prompted British media speculation - denied by Russia - that Moscow was downgrading diplomatic relations because of London's role as one of Ukraine's biggest supporters.
Poland joins anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine
Also on Friday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that Poland has joined an anti-ballistic missile coalition with Ukraine and other allies.
"From today, Poland is part of this major project... we agreed on the forms and frameworks of this cooperation," Tusk said in a video posted on X/Twitter.
Tusk attended a summit on Friday of a new regional grouping of eight Carpathian countries, held in western Ukraine and launched by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
Ukraine and nine European countries announced in July an air-defense coalition that would jointly develop a new anti-ballistic missile system as an alternative, cheaper solution to the US Patriot system.
Tusk told a press conference at the summit that Poland has prepared a new "significant" donation package for Ukraine, without giving further detail.
"I will be very consistent here. No one will change my opinion that Poland has to support Ukraine in its war against Russian aggression... History cannot divide us vis-à-vis Russia today," Tusk said.

articles.title: Landsbergis: Ukraine needs its own long-range deterrence to stay secure

Landsbergis: Ukraine needs its own long-range deterrence to stay secure
Former Lithuanian Foreign Minister Gabrielius Landsbergis expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
He noted that Ukraine has significantly increased its drone production during the years of the full-scale war, from several thousand to nearly 10 million annually. In the politician’s view, further scaling up these capabilities, combined with the development of missile systems, could fundamentally shift the balance of power.
Landsbergis stressed that building a comprehensive deterrence system requires not only weapons themselves but also the necessary infrastructure, including guidance systems and satellite capabilities.
“Add ballistic missiles to that. Good guidance systems, satellites and the like are also needed – to reach the point where, with or without allies, Ukraine can tell Putin: ‘Look, even if you try again next time, you will have no industry left,’” the politician said.
He believes Ukraine is uniquely positioned to establish such a system and that Western countries can help it achieve this.
“There is no other country that could do this – only Ukraine. And we, the West, are capable of helping Ukraine achieve it,” Landsbergis said.
At the same time, he believes Ukraine’s experience could also be used to strengthen the defenses of other countries potentially threatened by Russia.
Lithuania and other neighboring countries of Russia, in particular, could develop their own long-range deterrence systems adapted to their capabilities. According to the politician, this would allow countries in the region to rely not only on assistance from their allies but also on their own capabilities.
“That is what deterrence is – sovereign power,” Landsbergis emphasized.
As reported by Ukrinform, on September 18, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced during his visit to Ukraine that Poland had joined the Antiballistic Coalition.

articles.title: US and Denmark reach deal on Greenland, Trump says
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump claims 'infinite' Greenland security deal with Denmark
US President Donald Trump said Friday that he had struck a deal with Denmark to give Washington "permanent control" over Greenland's security that would bar Russia and China from setting up bases in the Arctic territory.
Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has repeatedly insisted that Washington needed to control Greenland for strategic reasons, alarming NATO ally Denmark and sparking fierce pushback from the alliance.
Denmark and Greenland -- an autonomous territory controlled by Copenhagen -- both hailed the deal and said they would sign it on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York next week.
"I am pleased to announce that the United States of America has entered into an Agreement with The Kingdom of Denmark, and Greenland, that gives the United States permanent control over security, and all other needs, in Greenland," Trump said on his Truth Social network.
"From now on, no US adversary can EVER have a base in Greenland, have a military presence in Greenland, or make sensitive investments in Greenland, without our express written approval."
The 80-year-old said it was an "'Infinite Life' Agreement, there is no end!" and said Washington would immediately start building up a large military presence in the territory.
'Good agreement'
Trump has repeatedly warned about Russia and China trying to establish a foothold in Greenland amid a strategic battle for supremacy in a warming Arctic, and the State Department left no doubt that they would not be allowed to do so.
"This agreement guarantees that China and Russia cannot have a base in Greenland, they cannot send troops to Greenland, and the necessary mechanisms are in place to prevent investment in sensitive sectors," a State Department official said.
At the Davos economic forum this past January, Trump reached a purported deal with NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte over the future of Greenland, the terms of which have remained vague.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen had said Monday that she was "optimistic" that ongoing discussions with the United States and Greenland since January could resolve the dispute.
On Friday, she said she was "pleased that there is a prospect of a good agreement for Greenland, the Kingdom of Denmark and the United States," adding that it was "good for NATO and Europe."
Greenland Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen said the deal with the United States "strengthens" the territory's security.
NATO tensions
Trump gave no details about how the deal would work, and it was not clear if it was linked to or substantially different from the Rutte deal.
But several media outlets have reported that the United States wants to open three new military bases in southern Greenland, in addition to the Pituffik base it already has in the north of the territory.
A 1951 defense pact, updated in 2004, already allows Washington to ramp up troop deployments and military installations on the island provided it informs Denmark and Greenland in advance.
At the height of the crisis, Trump would not rule out using force to seize the territory of 57,000 inhabitants, sowing anxiety within the EU and NATO.
Since then, tensions have cooled somewhat, and in an apparent move to assuage Trump, NATO launched a new mission to bolster security in the Arctic.

Russian authorities have reported attacks on the country’s voting systems and communication lines on the second day of a tightly controlled three-day-long parliamentary election.
Moscow’s electronic voting system was subjected to a powerful cyberattack overnight between Friday and Saturday, and the attack has continued, Interfax news agency reported.

Israel’s military focus extends beyond advanced fighter jets and next-generation stealth aircraft to space-based weapons and the development and production of interceptor aircraft, the outlet said.
Weapons to be demanded by Israeli officials also include "bunker-busting munitions and underground systems capable of operating deep beneath rocky mountains,” it added.

The package also includes 49 Pratt & Whitney F135-PW-100 engines, along with cryptographic equipment, electronic warfare support, training and logistics packages, according to a notification sent to the US Congress.
If completed, the deal would make Saudi Arabia the first Arab country to acquire F-35 fighter jets, while Israel is currently the only operator of the aircraft in the Middle East.
Israeli officials have repeatedly criticized Saudi Arabia over its refusal to normalize relations with Tel Aviv before the establishment of a Palestinian state along the 1967 borders, a condition which the international community supports while Israel continues to reject.

articles.title: Trump signs new Russia sanctions bill
articles.body:
Trump signs new Russia sanctions bill
US President Donald Trump has signed sweeping legislation expanding the sanctions on Russia and authorizing tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy. Moscow warned that additional sanctions would complicate efforts to settle the Ukraine conflict and could further destabilize the energy markets.
In a statement on Friday, the White House announced that Trump approved the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, after the Senate passed it 86-11 in August and the House passed it 262-159 on Wednesday.
The legislation targets senior Russian officials, banks, defense and energy entities, as well as what Western countries refer to as Russia’s ‘shadow fleet’ of ships. It also empowers Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest buyers of Russian crude oil and natural gas.
The text, however, does not explicitly name major Russian energy buyers such as China or India, and the tariff rate can be set below the 100% ceiling.
The measure was initially proposed by late Republican Senator and Russia hawk Lindsey Graham and Democrat Richard Blumenthal in April 2025. The original proposal threatened 500% tariffs on countries that buy Russian energy, but after more than a year of negotiations with the White House, the figure was cut to 100%.
The bill also grants Trump broad waiver powers, allowing him to suspend sanctions according to national interests and giving his administration wide leeway in setting tariff rates – one of the key points of negotiations between the White House and lawmakers, as some feared that the legislation would give Trump too much power.
The Trump administration recently eased sanctions on Russian oil. During the Iran war, the administration issued temporary exemptions allowing the sale and delivery of Russian oil already at sea to alleviate pressure on the energy markets.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov warned on Thursday that the “unfriendly” move “would definitely complicate efforts to find a peaceful settlement in Ukraine.”
The Russian Embassy in Washington argued that blocking Russian energy trade while Middle Eastern supplies are disrupted could prove costly for the US, calling it an “invitation to ever-higher prices at the pump.” It also warned that simultaneously escalating tensions with Moscow and Beijing would be a geopolitical lose-lose situation and would “only play into the hands of Euro-Atlantic warmongers.”

articles.title: Latvian defence technology companies meet German industry leaders in Berlin
articles.body:
During a trade mission organised by the Investment and Development Agency of Latvia (LIAA), Latvian defence and dual-use technology companies met leading German defence companies, industry organisations and a representative of the German Federal Ministry of Defence in Berlin. Members of the delegation, led by Latvian Minister for Economics Viktors Valainis, presented their solutions and discussed opportunities to join German companies’ supply chains, jointly develop technologies and expand production.
The programme focusing on defence and dual-use technologies began on 16 September with an event dedicated to cooperation between the Latvian and German defence industries, organised in partnership with the German Security and Defence Industry Association (BDSV).
“Industrial cooperation between Latvia and Germany is becoming increasingly close. In the first half of 2026, Latvia’s exports of goods to Germany grew by 10%, while exports of machinery, mechanical appliances and electrical equipment increased by EUR 34.3 million. This also represents the manufacturing base on which Latvia’s defence industry can grow. Our companies can supply electronic components, unmanned systems, military vehicles, metal structures and other solutions needed to strengthen Europe’s defence capabilities. The priority now is to involve Latvian companies more extensively in German and European supply chains, joint technology development and manufacturing,” Minister for Economics Viktors Valainis said.
Latvian business representatives met the leadership of BDSV, German defence companies and a representative of the German Federal Ministry of Defence to discuss industry priorities, upcoming procurements and opportunities for cooperation.
Direct talks with the German defence industry
During an in-depth industry session, Rheinmetall, HENSOLDT, Rohde & Schwarz and Quantum Systems presented their expertise and opportunities for cooperation. Discussions focused on expanding defence production and supply chains, sensors, electronic warfare and counter-unmanned aerial system solutions, secure communications and autonomous systems.
Latvia’s defence technology ecosystem was presented to German partners by Artis Pabriks, Executive Director of the Military Technology, Drone and Robotics Association MilTech Latvia, and Jānis Atslēns, a representative of the Federation of Security and Defence Industries of Latvia.
“As Ambassador, security is one of my main priorities in relations between Latvia and Germany. We cooperate both bilaterally and as NATO and EU partners. Germany is one of the world’s leading military industry countries, and Latvia has excellent opportunities to develop closer cooperation with the German defence industry. We have highly qualified specialists and innovative companies capable of adapting to changing industry conditions. Trust and close professional contacts form the foundation of this type of long-term cooperation. The Embassy will continue to actively support Latvian companies by helping them establish new contacts, strengthen their presence in the German market and become part of the European defence industry’s supply chains,” said Ilze Rūse, Latvia’s Ambassador to Germany.
Focus on unmanned and autonomous systems
On 17 September, Latvian and German companies, industry organisations and public-sector representatives participated in a round-table discussion on unmanned aerial vehicles and counter-UAV technologies, autonomous systems, robotics, artificial intelligence, secure communications, electronics and the resilience of defence supply chains. The event was organised by LIAA in cooperation with Berlin’s economic development agency Berlin Partner and MilTech Latvia.
Participants were introduced to the Latvian and Berlin defence technology ecosystems, while Latvian and German companies presented their solutions. The discussions explored specific areas for cooperation, including component supplies, systems integration, joint product development, technology testing and manufacturing.
“Economic cooperation between Latvia and Germany already has a solid foundation, with more than 1,000 German-owned companies operating in Latvia. In the defence industry, Latvian companies must now demonstrate their ability to meet specific technical, quality and delivery requirements. In Berlin, they had an opportunity to discuss these matters with potential partners and determine what steps are necessary to qualify as suppliers. Following the mission, LIAA will continue working on the most promising cooperation opportunities, advancing them towards technology testing, supplier qualification and cooperation agreements,” said Vita Balode-Andrūsa, Director of LIAA’s Export and Innovation Services Department.
Berlin is strengthening its position on Europe’s defence and security technology map. The city is home to approximately 130 companies specialising in security and defence, as well as more than 400 companies whose technologies can be used for both civilian and military purposes. The Berlin Senate is also developing a dedicated defence technology ecosystem to forge closer links between companies, researchers, investors and public-sector customers.
The delegation also visited Andres Industries AG, a Berlin-based company that develops and manufactures thermal imaging and night-vision technologies for armed forces, police and other security institutions.
Latvian companies offer technologies and manufacturing capacity
The Latvian delegation of defence and dual-use technology companies included ALMIKO, Daugavpils Lokomotīvju Remonta Rūpnīca, Electrify, EMJ Metāls, HansaMatrix, Latvia Packing, VOLBURG, VORX and VR Cars.
The delegation’s offering encompasses printed circuit board and electronics manufacturing, metalworking and the production of armoured structures, military ammunition packaging, materials for large-format 3D printing, military vehicles and unmanned ground platforms. In Germany, Latvian companies are seeking systems integrators, customers, manufacturing partners and opportunities to participate in German and broader European defence projects.
For example, Electrify presented the Latvian-developed Rocky6 electric unmanned ground platform in Berlin. It is designed to transport cargo and specialised equipment across difficult terrain, perform reconnaissance, evacuate casualties, and integrate communications and counter-UAV systems. The platform has a payload capacity of up to 1,200 kilograms and an electric range of up to 150 kilometres.
“Latvian defence technology companies offer their German partners a powerful combination of flexibility, engineering expertise and solutions tailored to real operational needs. At DK NEJET, we develop software-defined defence technologies, ranging from high-speed interceptors and navigation in GPS-denied environments to drone-swarm coordination. We combine engineering development, manufacturing and operator training within a single ecosystem. Combined with Germany’s industrial capacity, this creates a solid foundation for the rapid deployment of field-tested and cost-effective European defence solutions,” said DK NEJET co-founder Olga Provotar, emphasising the importance of participating in LIAA’s trade mission to Germany.
Trade mission covers several technology sectors
The Latvian business trade mission to Germany, organised by LIAA, took place from 14 to 17 September. It brought together 53 Latvian companies and organisations representing information and communication technologies, financial technologies, life sciences, and defence and dual-use technologies. The programme was organised by sector, combining company visits and joint events with individual business meetings.
Germany is Latvia’s largest export market outside the Baltic states. Since 2020, Latvia’s exports of goods and services to Germany have grown by more than 40%, rising from EUR 1.47 billion to approximately EUR 2.1 billion in 2025. Last year, Latvia exported more to Germany alone than to the United States, France and China combined.
Growth has continued this year: in the first half of 2026, exports to Germany increased by 11%, while Latvia’s total exports grew by 6%. Germany is also Latvia’s largest market for service exports, which reached EUR 779 million in 2025. More than 1,000 German-owned companies operate in Latvia, with their combined investments in share capital exceeding EUR 800 million.
LIAA organises participation in international trade missions under the European Union co-financed programme for the development of innovative entrepreneurship among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), supported by funding from the European Regional Development Fund and the Latvian state budget. Companies may participate in trade missions either for a fee or by receiving support to cover eligible costs.

articles.title: Germany receives first F-35 jet from US as NATO boosts military spending
articles.body:
Germany receives first F-35 jet from US as NATO boosts military spending
Germany received the first of nearly three dozen F-35 stealth warplanes it ordered four years ago from Lockheed Martin.
Germany has received its first F-35A Lightning II fighter jet, as the country accelerates a major military buildup and increases defence spending amid a broader push by European NATO members to strengthen their armed forces.
The delivery on Friday is part of Germany’s effort to fulfil NATO nuclear-sharing duties and modernise its military after decades of relatively low defence spending.
Lockheed Martin formally presented the aircraft to the German government during a ceremony at its production facility in Fort Worth, Texas, attended by German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius.
“This is the beginning of a new era for the German Air Force: the new F-35A fighter jet is the world’s most advanced combat aircraft,” Pistorius said in a statement. “It is characterised by its stealth capabilities, close integration with other platforms, and exceptionally powerful sensor technology.”
Germany ordered 35 F-35As in 2022, the year Russia launched its invasion of Ukraine. The aircraft are intended to replace Germany’s ageing Tornado fleet.
The Trump administration has long pressured Europe to spend more on defence, allowing Washington to focus on other challenges such as countering China.
European countries, including Germany, are ramping up military budgets as a result, agreeing in 2025 to Trump’s demand to devote five percent of GDP to security-related spending by 2035.

Yemen’s Houthi group has claimed it launched missile and drone attacks on “sensitive targets” in the Saudi capital Riyadh alongside a separate attack on facilities of oil firm Saudi Aramco in coastal Yanbu.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on US social media company X on Friday that the group carried out two operations using “a large number of ballistic and cruise missiles as well as drones.”
He said the first operation targeted “sensitive targets” in Riyadh, while the second targeted Saudi Aramco in the western coastal city of Yanbu.

On July 20, the Houthis announced what they called a “maritime blockade” on Saudi Arabia before later claiming missile and drone attacks on Saudi-linked vessels and sites.

articles.title: Russia reportedly buries its drone factory underground
articles.body:
- Ukrainian analyst Dnipro Osint said Russia has built about 42,000 square meters of underground production space for Shahed/Geran drones at Alabuga.
- The claim follows confirmed satellite evidence of new production halls, a 340-hectare site expansion, and defensive towers built around the facility in 2026.
Russia has begun building underground production space for its Shahed and Geran attack drones at the Alabuga industrial zone in Tatarstan, according to Ukrainian open-source intelligence analyst Dnipro Osint, who estimated roughly 42,000 square meters of underground area has already been constructed there.
Dnipro Osint said the shift underground appears to have followed earlier Ukrainian strikes on the Alabuga site, and that Russia has been expanding the underground infrastructure quickly since then.
The analyst placed the activity at coordinates 55.808719°, 52.026664°, within the broader Alabuga Special Economic Zone near the city of Yelabuga, roughly 1,200 km (750 miles) from the Ukrainian border. This specific underground construction claim comes from a single open-source analyst and has not yet been independently confirmed through separate satellite imagery analysis.
Alabuga is Russia’s primary production site for the Geran-2, a Russian-built version of Iran’s Shahed-136 one-way attack drone that Russian forces fire at Ukrainian cities on a near-nightly basis. The facility has grown substantially over the past year. Satellite imagery cited by Radio Liberty showed the zone’s footprint expanded by 340 hectares between May 2025 and May 2026, with new hangars, dormitories for foreign workers, and a roughly 450-hectare construction area added south of the M-12 highway. Ukrainian analysts reported on Sept. 14 that five additional production halls had gone up in the southern part of the site, based on satellite images similarly sourced from Dnipro Osint.
Russia has also added physical protection around the plant. Satellite images from July and August analyzed by Spencer Faragasso of the Institute for Science and International Security showed a two-ring system of lattice towers under construction around Alabuga’s production buildings, an arrangement meant to complicate future drone or missile strikes on the site.
Dnipro Osint said the combined effect of these changes, underground construction, dispersed production buildings and added physical defenses, is making Russia’s drone manufacturing base progressively harder and more expensive to target. The site relies heavily on foreign labor recruited through the Alabuga Polytechnic College and other channels; the United Kingdom sanctioned 35 entities and individuals in May 2026 over recruitment tied to the facility, and the site remains under separate U.S. and European Union sanctions.

articles.title: Russia’s next-gen Armata tank remains stuck a decade after debut
articles.body:
- New dashcam footage this week showed a Russian T-14 Armata tank crossing toward a firing range, with no new program details released.
- Russia has built roughly 20 T-14s against an original 2,300-tank target, and continues to rely on upgraded T-90M tanks for the war in Ukraine.
New dashcam footage circulating on Russian state-aligned media this week shows a T-14 Armata tank crossing a dirt road toward a firing range, the latest glimpse of a next-generation tank program that has spent a decade struggling to move beyond testing.
No new technical details accompanied the footage, and it does not appear to show anything beyond a routine range exercise. The clip, recorded from a passing civilian vehicle’s dashcam, adds to a long pattern of brief, unofficial sightings that have periodically resurfaced online since the T-14 was first unveiled during rehearsals for Russia’s 2015 Victory Day parade.
The T-14 represented a sharp break from Soviet-era tank design when Uralvagonzavod introduced it, built around an unmanned turret, a separately armored crew capsule, and the Afghanit active protection system meant to intercept incoming projectiles before they hit the vehicle. Russia originally planned to build more than 2,300 of the tanks by 2020. A decade later, estimates put the actual number built at roughly 20, most of them prototypes or pre-production vehicles rather than a true production run.
Cost has been the central obstacle. Estimates for the T-14 range from about $8 million to $15 million per vehicle, compared with $1.5 million to $2.5 million for an upgraded T-90M, the tank Russia has relied on instead throughout its war in Ukraine. Despite repeated claims from Russian officials and pro-government media that the T-14 has seen combat, no independently verified evidence has emerged confirming it ever fought at the front. Russian media reported in mid-2023 that a small number of Armatas reached Ukraine and fired from standoff range before being withdrawn within months, but outside analysts were never able to confirm those claims. British defense intelligence assessed at the time that Russian troops were reluctant to accept the tanks into service and that any deployment would likely serve propaganda purposes rather than combat need.
Even Rostec, the state conglomerate that oversees the T-14’s development, has acknowledged the program’s limits. Rostec chief executive Sergey Chemezov told Russian state news agency in March 2024 that while the Armata outperformed everything else in Russia’s inventory, it was too expensive to field at scale, and that the war would instead be fought with upgraded T-90Ms and refurbished T-72s. Uralvagonzavod, the world’s largest tank plant and the T-14’s manufacturer, has since turned much of its production capacity toward exactly that work, rebuilding older T-72 hulls and building new T-90Ms rather than expanding Armata output.
Some Russian defense industry figures have floated a different path forward, arguing that individual technologies developed for the T-14, its firepower, protection or mobility systems, could be transferred into the more widely fielded T-90M and T-72 rather than fielding the Armata itself in large numbers. Russia has also offered to transfer T-14 technology to India for local production under that country’s domestic manufacturing program, though that arrangement has not produced any confirmed manufacturing to date.
Analysts who track the program have grown increasingly skeptical of its future. Long development timelines and design choices that outside experts say have not kept pace with battlefield lessons from Ukraine have led some to describe the Armata as functionally dead on arrival as a mass-production tank, even as isolated footage like this week’s clip keeps the program in public view.

articles.title: USA to Sell Ukraine S-300 Clone Missiles
articles.body:
The United States has approved the sale of S-300 Clone missiles to Ukraine as part of a new package of equipment and weapons.
Apart from a mention in the U.S. State Department’s list, no further information about these missiles has been provided.
Their purchase will be financed by European partners and through funds from the U.S. Foreign Military Financing (FMF) program.
The then-U.S. Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin first spoke about work on new missiles for the air defense system back in September 2024.
At a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in Ramstein, he announced joint work with Ukraine on developing a ‘replacement’ for the Soviet S-300 air defense systems and R-27 air-to-air missiles.
“With the support of several European companies, the United States is working with Ukraine to develop and manufacture a replacement for the S-300 surface-to-air missile system, as well as the R-27 air-to-air missile,” Austin said.
In August 2026, Robert Hamilton, a retired U.S. Army colonel and president of the Delphi Global Research Center, spoke about the joint development of new missiles.
According to him, the project involves the production of 100–200 anti-aircraft missiles per year.
In addition to work on developing missiles in collaboration with partners, there are also reports of localization efforts in Ukraine. Localization involves bringing European partners on board the project.
Prior to the start of the Russian invasion in 2022, Ukraine had approximately 25–30 battalions of S-300PT/PS systems at its disposal, in varying states of operational readiness.
The systems currently deployed in Ukraine are designed to counter strategic and tactical aircraft, as well as cruise missiles, at altitudes ranging from 25 m to 27 km and at ranges of up to 100 km.
On April 8, 2022, the then-Prime Minister of Slovakia, Eduard Heger, announced the provision of an additional S-300PMU air defense system to Ukraine, which had been in service with his country.
During combat operations, certain components (launchers and radars) were lost, and Ukraine’s missile stockpiles were depleted. For this reason, partners—including Norway—allocated funds for Ukraine to purchase missiles from third countries. However, a shortage persists.

articles.title: US troop deaths during Iran war exceed Pentagon count by at least four
articles.body:
US troop deaths during Iran war exceed Pentagon count by at least four
WASHINGTON – More US troops have died during the US-Israeli war with Iran than the Pentagon has publicly disclosed, the Washington Post reported on Sept 18.
Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth denied the report.
The Post, citing five unidentified officials, reported that there had been at least 22 military fatalities, four more than were listed in the data available on the Pentagon’s public database.
The newspaper also reported, citing another unidentified official, that not all of the undisclosed deaths were directly tied to the months-long conflict but involved US personnel who were in the Middle East amid ongoing hostilities.
Hegseth, in a post on social media platform X, called the report “a complete LIE”.
The Post did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In its story, the newspaper said the Pentagon had declined to address its questions about the discrepancy in casualty accounting. REUTERS
